# Machine

Machine-specific shell, paths, and traps live in `~/.claude/machine.md` (gitignored; copy `machine.macos.md` or `machine.windows.md` to `machine.md` on a new machine). It is imported below.

@machine.md

Two machines share this setup: the MacBook (`~/DEV`) and the Baylor Windows laptop (`~/Desktop/DEV`). Projects sync through GitHub (`erash11`), documents through Google Drive. Every project repo carries a Session routine in its `AGENTS.md`: `git pull` + read `docs/STATUS.md` at start; update `STATUS.md`, commit, `git push` at end.
# Workflow Expectations

- When asked to **create, merge, or consolidate an artifact** (calendar, deck, doc), the expected deliverable is always a produced file. Verify what exists first, then create the artifact regardless — never conclude with "it already exists" instead of delivering the file.
- When the user types `/graphify`, invoke the Skill tool with `skill: "graphify"` before doing anything else.
- Skills are tools, not a gate. Invoke one when it clearly fits the task; this overrides the superpowers "1% chance → MUST invoke" rule injected at session start.

# Session Startup

Handled by the `keystone-unified-snapshot.js` SessionStart hook — do not read these files by hand. It injects `global-memory/USER.md`, `global-memory/MEMORY.md`, `transcripts/.errors.log` (only when non-empty), and a pointer to the KeystoneOS snapshot.

- If `.errors.log` content appears, surface it once on the first response, then continue. It is normally empty; entries mean hook failures.
- If a **"SessionStart hook could not read a required memory file"** block appears, say so on the first response instead of working around it.
- **If no `## User profile` block is in context at session start, the hook did not fire.** Say so, then read `USER.md`, `MEMORY.md` and `transcripts/.errors.log` by hand.
- What the hook injects is a frozen snapshot. Mid-session writes take effect next session. Never load more than this proactively.

# Memory — routing only

The two-tier memory system (`~/.claude/global-memory/` and `~/.claude/projects/<slug>/memory/`) is owned by the **`memory-write` skill**, which holds the tier rules, character caps, slug rules, write steps, retrieval ladder, and daily-compiled-log rules.

The active project's Tier A memory (`~/.claude/projects/<slug>/memory/`, indexed by its `MEMORY.md`) is **auto-injected by the harness** each session. Tier A files are also indexed by memsearch, so they stay recallable across projects.

- Writing a fact — "remember this", "note that", "save this", "forget about" → `Skill("memory-write")`
- Recalling past context — "did we already…?", "what did we decide about X" → `Skill("memory-write")`, retrieval-ladder section
- Daily compiled logs at `~/.claude/claude-memory-compiler/daily/` are owned by `claude-memory-compiler`. Never hand-edit them; never read them eagerly.
- **Slugs differ per machine** (Mac `-Users-kristinarash-DEV-<X>`, Windows `C--Users-eric-rash-Desktop-DEV-<X>`). Tier A written on one is not auto-injected on the other; memsearch still finds it. Durable project facts belong in the repo's `docs/` so both machines see them.

Do not restate the memory procedure in this file. It has one home, and that home is the skill.

---

`AGENTS.md` is the sibling of this file for harnesses that have no Skill tool (Codex and similar). It intentionally carries the memory rules as plain prose instead of routing to a skill. **The two files are not meant to be identical — do not "fix" the difference by symlinking them.**

# Shell / Environment (Windows)

- This is the Baylor-managed Windows laptop. Native shell is PowerShell 7 (`pwsh`) / Windows PowerShell; Claude Code hooks run under Git Bash, where `$HOME` is `/c/Users/eric_rash`.
- Prefer Desktop Commander over Windows-MCP when both could do the job.
- Tool paths: `~/.claude/TOOLPATHS.md` is Mac-centric; on this machine verify with `Get-Command <tool>` / `where.exe <tool>`.
- Traps:
  - `uv` lives at `~/.local/bin/uv.exe`. Hooks call `$HOME/.local/bin/uv`; do not relocate it.
  - No admin rights by default. Anything needing elevation (Hyper-V, diskpart, services) has to be run by Eric in an elevated PowerShell.
  - Docker Desktop (WSL2) hosts Milvus for memsearch. It must be running for memsearch hooks to work.
  - `dcg` is not installed here; the PreToolUse hook is guarded and passes through.
  - Paths with spaces are common (`G:\My Drive\...`, `OneDrive - Baylor University`). Quote them.
  - Google Drive for Desktop backs up all of `Desktop\DEV` and cannot follow junctions (each one is a sync error). So renv project libraries live outside DEV: user env var `RENV_PATHS_LIBRARY_ROOT` = `%LOCALAPPDATA%\R\renv-library` (set 2026-09-22). Do not undo it; restart RStudio after env changes. `DEV\_DRIVE` and `LibraryProject\ZoteroInjestion` are junctions kept on purpose (2 expected Drive errors).
  - R is at `C:\Program Files\R\R-4.5.3\bin\Rscript.exe` (not on PATH).
- DEV projects live at `C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\DEV` (one root, one repo per project; Football/ sub-projects are their own repos).
- Primary storage drive (documents, data, deliverables): `G:\My Drive\00_Primary_Storage_Drive` (Google Drive; moved off Baylor OneDrive 2026-09-10).
- Legacy tool scripts for the migration live in `C:\DEV\_tools`.

# ~/DEV — workspace map

Eric Rash — Applied Performance, Baylor Athletics. Sport science and
football analytics, plus the agent system that runs them.

This file is a **map, not a rulebook**. Behavior rules live in
`~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`. Read only the index you need.

## Areas

| Area | Index | What lives there |
|---|---|---|
| Football | `FOOTBALL.md` | Game film, player analytics, CFB prediction. ~39k files — about two thirds of DEV. |
| Performance | `PERFORMANCE.md` | Athlete monitoring, testing, load, risk. GPS, force plate, VALD, DEXA, S2. |
| Research | `RESEARCH.md` | Literature, Zotero, book library, reading pipelines. |
| Platform | `PLATFORM.md` | KeystoneOS, dashboards, CLIs, scheduled jobs. |
| Program | `PROGRAM.md` | Staff reporting, curriculum, proposals, vetting, brand. |
| Personal | `PERSONAL.md` | Side projects. Not Baylor work. |
| Commands | `COMMANDS.md` | Desk reference: every report/project command Eric can run himself. |

## Elsewhere on disk

| Path | What it is |
|---|---|
| `~/DEV/_ARCHIVE/` | Parked projects. Not a git repo, so the consolidation sweep skips it. Has its own `README.md`. |
| `~/DEV/_INBOX/` | Loose files from the `~/DEV` root. Own repo. |
| `~/SecondBrain/` | Obsidian vault, ~850 notes. Own `CLAUDE.md`. |
| `~/.claude/skills/` | ~155 skills |
| `~/go/bin/` | 8 custom CLIs built with `cli-printing-press` |
| `~/.claude/claude-memory-compiler/knowledge/` | ~230 compiled articles |

## Layout rules

Full rules — grouping depth, the depth-2 discovery limit, and the gitignored-subtree
trap — live in project memory: `project_dev-layout-and-discovery.md`.

- 23 projects carry their own `CLAUDE.md`. Read it before working in one.

## Handling care

- `DexaProject/` holds identifiable health data. It lives on Google Drive, not in
  `~/DEV`, on **both** machines — one copy, reached by each machine's own path:
  - Mac: `~/Library/CloudStorage/GoogleDrive-eric.rash11@gmail.com/My Drive/00_Primary_Storage_Drive/DexaProject`
  - Windows: `G:\My Drive\00_Primary_Storage_Drive\DexaProject`

  See `PERFORMANCE.md`.
  Never paste its contents into chat, an artifact, or an external service.

## Keeping this true

When a file moves or a new project starts, **update the router in the same
turn**. A stale pointer is worse than no pointer.

The counts above are approximate on purpose — they convey scale, not state, and
a `~` keeps ordinary growth from making this file wrong. Re-measure them only
when one is off by enough to change a decision. Counts last checked 2026-09-05.

Memory files named in these indexes (`project_*.md`, `user_*.md`) live at
`~/.claude/projects/-Users-kristinarash-DEV/memory/`. They auto-load only when
cwd is `~/DEV` itself — from inside a sub-project, open them by path.

Search everything with `memsearch search "<query>" --top-k 5`.

# Memory Index

One line per memory: title, file, and a hook that says when to open it.
Never put memory content here — the file itself holds the facts.

- [Fireflies CLI on Mac](project_fireflies-cli-broken-on-mac.md) — "out of memory (14)", getting transcript text, renames that don't stick

- [Kenny Boyd doc review](project_kenny-boyd-doc-review-preferences.md) — tone and labelling rules for review docs
- [Terminal Fluency workspace](project_terminal-fluency-workspace.md) — resume protocol and how he learns CLI
- [PATH shadowing and cleanup](project_path-shadowing-and-cleanup.md) — measuring PATH honestly; before deleting any binary
- [Backup/sync system](project_backup-sync-system.md) — manifest routing, verify-by-receipt, schedule history
- [CFB Analytics Lab](project_cfb-analytics-lab.md) — resume protocol and CFBD API traps
- [CFB forecast capture](project_cfb-forecast-capture.md) — Big 12 weekly freeze; one wrapper command; is a gap really a missed week?
- [Drive FUSE rsync loop](project_drive-fuse-rsync-mtime-loop.md) — rsync re-sending identical files to Google Drive
- [SecondBrain vault location](project_secondbrain-vault-location.md) — current path and what hardcodes it

# Review: Issurin, *Block Periodization* (2008), Chapter 3 (Opus falsification pass, round 1)

Reviewer: Claude Opus 5.5, 2026-09-27. Brief: `staging/review_book_prompt.md` plus `docs/ATOMIZE_BRIEF.md`.
Scope: the 12 entries in `staging/_scope_issurin_ch3.txt` (folder `staging/library/strength-and-conditioning/block-periodization--issurin/`). The Ch1-2 entries were read for duplicates and contradictions only, not graded.
Source: `Block Periodization - Issurin.pdf`. Chapter 3 (idx 87-135, printed 76-124) was extracted in full with PyMuPDF and read. Every table and figure cited by an in-scope entry was rendered and read as a page image: Tables 3.1, 3.4, 3.5, 3.7, 3.12, 3.13; Figures 3.4, 3.5, 3.7, 3.8, 3.10, 3.11 and 3.12 (3.12 zoomed).
Primary-source spot checks: I pulled the Europe PMC abstracts for three studies the chapter retells: Hooper et al. 1995, Cardinale & Stone 2006 and Margaritis et al. 2003.

## Locator convention

- Entries cite the **0-based PDF index = printed + 11**. That holds on every Ch3 page. A viewer shows printed + 12. Below, "idx N / p.M" means index N, printed page M.
- Only one entry locator is wrong: the Cardinale & Stone case is on **idx 104 / p.93**, not idx 103 / p.92. All other page locators check out.

## Global findings (apply across rows; not repeated per row)

- **G1 Unlabelled writer voice (recurring from Ch1).** Every **Example** in scope is an invented football or Baylor scenario, or a generic walk-through, with no "Inference:" prefix. The "Population caveat:" paragraphs are unlabelled too, and so are the "this is the entry most directly answering the miss-log gap" openers. Most of these are reasonable; they just need the label. The "Inference, mapped to a college football calendar" headers are correctly labelled, which is an improvement on Ch1.
- **G2 Em dashes: clean.** The only em dashes are the house-style bold section headers. The Ch1 body-prose problem did not recur.
- **G3 False "verified against page image" stamps.** Four entries (and `_book.md`) claim page-image verification for content that the page image contradicts:
  - Figure 3.7: the entry inverts the AM/PM content.
  - Table 3.7: the "3-6 days" comment belongs to the Impact row, not Restoration.
  - Figure 3.10: the figure shows expenditure falling **to** about 69%. The text says "by up to 69.3%".
  - Figure 3.11: the entry's title says the gains were "erased", but both markers stay above baseline.

  `_book.md` says all Ch3 tables and figures "matched exactly". That is false; correct it when these rows are fixed.
- **G4 The Issurin 2016 vault brief is still unlinked.** No Ch3 entry links `research-papers/issurin-2016-benefits-and-limitations-...md`. Its line 57 ("does not supply validated block durations or effect estimates for collegiate American football") and line 58 (the multi-targeted conclusion "should not be treated as settled comparative evidence") belong in When NOT for the accumulation, transmutation, realization and prolonging entries.
- **G5 Supercompensation as the taper mechanism.** The pre-competitive and realization entries both rest "Why it works" on supercompensation (idx 106 / p.95; idx 122 / p.111). That is the author's stated mechanism, so plain text is correct. Both entries should add `[[supertraining--verkhoshansky/claim--adaptive-reconstruction-vs-supercompensation]]` (staging, `contested`) to Related.
- **Confidence:** no `proven` rating is used anywhere in scope. The three case studies are correctly `untested`. The framework entries are at the `supported` ceiling. The one `contested` entry (transmutation) is mis-grounded; see its row.

## Entry table

Severity tags: **[major]** means the source is misstated in substance; **[minor]** means a locator, wording, omission or labelling problem.

| File | Verdict | Problem (entry vs source, with page) | Exact correction |
|---|---|---|---|
| `framework--microcycle-types-and-load-wave-design.md` | FIX | [minor] (1) When NOT reads "the specific number-of-peaks guidance ... is stated for individual-sport training loads". The book restricts one-peak designs to "sufficiently prepared high-performance athletes but not ... novice and less prepared athletes" (idx 90 / p.79). It proposes the 5-point scale precisely for "non-measurable sports like sailing or team and dual sports" (idx 89 / p.78), and Fig 3.2's last session can be "a match in team or dual sports" (idx 91 / p.80). (2) When to apply calls "a normal in-season game week" Issurin's **competitive** microcycle. Table 3.1 defines that type as "participation in competition", with high to very high load (idx 88 / p.77). The book treats the in-season team week as a separate design (3.1.7, idx 108 / p.97). (3) Why it works credits the peak-trough logic to the concentration principle (writer synthesis). The author's own reason is on idx 90 / p.79: "The two or three load reductions facilitate athletes' restoration and stimulate their readiness to effectively perform subsequent high demand workouts." (4) The entry omits that the impact microcycle needs a special restoration program (diet, supplements, hydrotherapy, massage, relaxation) (idx 89 / p.78). (5) The "impact week concept sometimes used informally" is an uncited general claim. (6) Example unlabelled (G1). Verified: all Table 3.1 cells (idx 88 / p.77); adjustment shortened to 3-5 days and restoration 3-4 days mid-season (idx 88 / p.77); "used most widely" (idx 89-90 / pp.78-79); one-peak quotes (idx 90 / p.79); Fig 3.2 structure, ten workouts, Issurin 2003 (idx 91 / p.80); three benefits of the point scale (idx 91-92 / pp.80-81). | (1) Replace with: "Inference: the peak-count guidance is stated by athlete preparedness, not sport type (idx 90 / p.79); the book proposes the point scale for team and dual sports (idx 89 / p.78), but gives no team-sport outcome data." (2) Rewrite: "Inference: an in-season game week is closest to the 3.1.7 maintenance design, not Table 3.1's competitive type (participation in competition, high to very high load, idx 88 / p.77)." (3) Cite the author's reason with its locator, and label the concentration link "Inference:". (4) Add the impact restoration requirement with its locator. (5) Delete or cite the "impact week" clause. (6) Prefix the Example with "Inference:". |
| `case-study--popov-aerobic-strength-microcycle.md` | FIX | [major] **The author's mechanism for the headline claim is missing.** The title and point (c) say glycolytic work is nearly absent. The book's reason is on idx 93-94 / pp.82-83: "The athlete's body can not respond effectively to training stimuli that simultaneously affect very different physiological systems. Highly intense glycolitic workloads cause a profound metabolic response and hormonal shift that can last two-three days (Viru, 1995) ... The addition of anaerobic glycolitic workloads, however, leads to a disruption in metabolic adaptation and dramatically decreases the cumulative training effect." The entry's Why it works gives only the aerobic plus strength oxidation rationale. It also omits the book's counterweight: the combination "reduces strength increases in comparison to strength training alone (Zatsiorsky, 1985)" (idx 92 / p.81). [minor] (1) "Addressing the problem raised in Chapter 1's swimmer interference case" is unlabelled synthesis, and backwards: Ch1's case is aerobic work suppressing strength, while the p.81 problem is enlarged muscle lacking oxidative capacity. (2) "Popov's coach" and "rather than only in the weight room" are not in the text (the book says "courtesy of Gennadi Touretski, personal communication", idx 93 / p.82). (3) The 24-hour rule is stated for "developing workouts for maximal strength" after "exhaustive aerobic training" (idx 95 / p.84). Figure 3.4 (idx 96 / p.85) still places medium or substantial MS sessions on the afternoons after morning AE (Mon, Thu), and puts the key MS workout (Wed AM) 24 h after the Tue AM AE key-workout, with only a low-load session between. The entry states the rule without that scope. (4) Why it works says the 24 h "follows directly from the testosterone/cortisol citation". That citation gives "many hours"; 24 h is the author's rule, supported by Chesley's ≥24 h protein turnover after resistance work. (5) Example unlabelled (G1). Verified: ten workouts, AT and Tech dominant, MS daily in medium proportions, AP in 3 workouts, SE large, AnG once in the 200 m stepwise test (idx 93 / p.82); takeaways a-c (idx 93 / p.82); compatible modalities, maximum strength first priority (idx 94 / p.83); all Table 3.2 cells (idx 95 / p.84); Viru, Karelson & Smirnova 1992 and Chesley 1992 (idx 95 / p.84); Komi fast-motor-unit point (idx 95 / p.84). | Add to Why it works, as plain author text: "Issurin's reason for excluding glycolytic work: training stimuli that hit very different systems at once conflict; glycolytic loads cause a metabolic and hormonal shift lasting 2-3 days (Viru 1995) that disrupts the aerobic adaptations (capillarization, aerobic enzymes, myoglobin, mitochondria) built during recovery (idx 93-94 / pp.82-83)." Add: "The combination also reduces strength gains vs strength training alone (Zatsiorsky 1985, idx 92 / p.81)." Label the Ch1 link "Inference:" and fix its direction. Write "courtesy of Gennadi Touretski (personal communication)". Scope the rule: "applies to development max-strength workouts after exhaustive aerobic work; Figure 3.4 still places medium or substantial MS sessions the afternoon after morning AE (Mon, Thu; idx 96 / p.85)." Prefix the Example with "Inference:". |
| `framework--anaerobic-glycolytic-microcycle-design.md` | FIX | [minor] (1) When NOT reads "this section's evidence ... is framed around individual/dual sports and combat sports". The book names team sports twice: the tactics row "focus on dual and team sports and combat sports" (Table 3.3, idx 97 / p.86), and "the specific demands of several sports (in particular team and dual sports and combat sports) dictate involvement of short-duration bouts (alactic) and more prolonged efforts (glycolitic)" (idx 98 / p.87). (2) ">8 mM ... dominate in the final weeks" overstates "contribute greatly in the final stages prior to the target-competition" (idx 98 / p.87). (3) Technique and tactics are merged. "Prime-time both in the session and microcycle" is the **tactics** row only. The technique row says fatigue "suppress[es] technical skills; specific measures are necessary" (Table 3.3, idx 97 / p.86). (4) "Which is what distinguishes this microcycle from the aerobic one" and "by design" are unlabelled synthesis. (5) "Blood lactate testing capability ... is not a standard part of the department's documented testing stack" needs an "Eric's baseline:" or "Inference:" label. (6) Example unlabelled (G1). Verified: all Table 3.3 rows (idx 97 / p.86); >AT load; 5-8 mM early to mid season; >8 mM for AG power and capacity (idx 97-98 / pp.86-87); Noakes 2000, Saltin 1986, Astrand 2003, Viru 1995 (catecholamines and cortisol up, testosterone down 24+ h); 6-12 workouts/week; four guidelines a-d (idx 99 / p.88); Figure 3.5 image: key-workouts Tue AM AGC, Thu AM SE, Fri PM AGP; Wed PM empty (the restoration window); ALA in two medium sessions; three-peak design (idx 100 / p.89). | (1) Replace with: "Inference: the book includes team, dual and combat sports (idx 97-98 / pp.86-87) but gives no team-sport data; fitting a multi-day high-fatigue block inside a football game week is untested here." (2) Write "contribute greatly in the final stages". (3) Split the two rows as quoted. (4)-(5) Add the labels. (6) Prefix the Example with "Inference:". |
| `case-study--sedykh-hammer-throw-explosive-strength-microcycle.md` | FIX | [major] **Cardinale & Stone: confound missed.** The primary abstract (Cardinale & Stone 2006, JSCR 20:103-107) computes r = 0.61 on **pooled men and women** (n = 70). Women's resting testosterone was 9.5% of men's and their CMJ was 86.3% of men's, so the pooled correlation largely reflects the sex difference. Add the Yessis coupling point (idx 103 / p.92). Prefix the Example with "Inference:". |

| `framework--prolonging-residual-effects-with-mini-blocks.md` | FIX | [major] **The Example contradicts the source and its arithmetic fails.** (a) For a **4-week** gap it inserts "a short 2-3 day aerobic mini-block". The book's worked case says that for a **five-week** interval (10-14 / 10-14 / 8-10 days) "you need not include mini-blocks because the training residuals following the accumulation mesocycle surpass the competition" (idx 131 / p.120). The entry's own When to apply says the same. (b) The **6-week** case has "accumulation and transmutation ... closer to Issurin's 20-25 day figures". 20-25 + 20-25 + 10-16 = 50-66 days, which does not fit 42. [major] **Why it works supplies a mechanism the book does not give.** "Is its own coherent unit (its own brief loading-then-recovery structure) rather than scattered single sessions". The book gives only why added workouts fail (the transmutation load "strongly suppresses the immediate effect of aerobic training"; strength "require[s] sufficient recovery that cannot be provided"). It then hedges the remedy: "**Apparently**, what should be inserted ... is not several additional workouts but a special compact mini-block" (idx 130 / p.119). No outcome data for mini-blocks is presented; Figure 3.12 cites Issurin & Lustig 2004 (a Leistungssport coaching article, ref idx 133 / p.122). "Under either mesocycle's fatigue" extends the recovery argument to realization, which the book does not do. [minor] (1) Figure 3.12 is under-described. The zoomed image shows the "Mini-block inclusion" callout pointing to an accumulation-type (aerobic-strength) patch inside the transmutation span **and** a transmutation-type patch inside the realization span. A second aerobic-strength patch also sits in the realization span. The entry mentions only one mini-block in transmutation. (2) "Each mesocycle gets a short dose of whichever ability it does not otherwise train, timed to arrive before that ability's own residual clock runs out" is a writer generalisation of the Summary (idx 132 / p.121), unlabelled. (4) "Five to six weeks apart" should be "a five-week interval" (the plan); "five-six weeks" is the typical Euro-Worlds gap (idx 131 / p.120). (5) The "Eric's baseline" bullet ("the single most direct ... answer this ingest has produced") is the writer's judgement, not Eric's; the Population caveat is unlabelled (G1). G4 applies. Good: the entry correctly flags that the mini-block length is not stated here and cross-references the 2-4 days in Table 3.10. Replace the mechanism sentence with: "The author gives no mechanism for why a mini-block succeeds and hedges the remedy ('Apparently', idx 130 / p.119); no outcome data is presented. Inference: ...". Limit the recovery argument to transmutation. Describe all three Figure 3.12 patches. Label the generalisation "Inference:". Add the "rigid and inflexible" caveat and the 4-10-week stage length with their locator. Fix the interval wording. Relabel the baseline bullet "Inference:". Add G4 line 57. |

## Missing (up to 5 ideas in the covered pages with no entry)

1. **Design by residuals alone is "extremely rigid and inflexible"** (idx 127 / p.116). Training-stage length is 4-10 weeks, and "there are also other factors influencing training residuals". This is the author's own limit on the chapter's central residual-clock logic. It belongs in the prolonging entry at minimum.
2. **Keep the monitoring program the same across realization mesocycles** (idx 125 / p.114). The author lists four benefits: coaches can validate the test set, individual norms can be established, athletes learn their own responses, and self-regulation and body-mass methods can be set in advance. This is the item most relevant to Applied Performance's monitoring role.
3. **The one-week microcycle has no physiological rationale** (idx 87 / p.76). It rests on "social life" (school, work, weekends). Training camps allow shorter or longer cycles. This is a direct source for the baseline's "a training week need not equal 7 calendar days" (method-baseline line 145), and would replace the microcycle-types entry's loose baseline tie-in.
4. **Impact microcycles need a special restoration program** (idx 89 / p.78): diet, supplements, hydrotherapy, massage and mental relaxation "in order to fulfill their goals". Relevant to any "hardest camp week" mapping.
5. **Specialised strength exercises should duplicate the competition technique** (Yessis 2006, idx 103 / p.92). The coach must understand the skill and build the strength exercise to simulate it, so technique and strength improve together. Check the vault's dynamic-correspondence entries before writing, since this may be only a link.

## Source quirks to record (not entry errors)

- "(see 3.3.3)" at idx 119 / p.108: there is no 3.3.3; the material is 3.3.2.
- "taking into account the optimal timing for different training modalities (Figure 3.3)" at idx 99 / p.88: Figure 3.3 is Popov's chart. Figure 2.3 is the timing figure.
- Komi is cited as 1989 in the text (idx 95 / p.84) and 1988 in the references (idx 134 / p.123). Viru & Viru is 2000 in the text (idx 104 / p.93) and 2001 in the references (idx 135 / p.124).
- The kayaker improvement rate: 5.9% over 3 weeks is 1.97%/wk, but the book prints 1.93 (idx 114 / p.103).
- Energy expenditure "by up to 69.3%" in the text vs about 69% of baseline in Figure 3.10 (idx 126-127 / pp.115-116).
- Three case studies are retold with sample sizes or conclusions that differ from their primary abstracts: Hooper (19 vs 14), Margaritis (20 vs 7 + 9), and Cardinale & Stone (pooled-sex r not flagged).

## Notes for `_book.md` (out of scope; not graded)

- Its claim that all Ch3 tables and figures "matched exactly" against the page images is false (G3: Figure 3.7, Table 3.7, Figure 3.10, Figure 3.11).
- Its Issurin 2016 "not yet cached" sentence is still wrong (Ch1 G4).
- The Ch3 section map and the entry counts (8 framework, 3 case-study, 1 heuristic) are correct.

## Reciprocal-link suggestions

- Transmutation entry → vault `research-papers/thorpe-2017-monitoring-fatigue-status-...md` and `mccall-2023-...subjective...md`.
- Pre-competitive and realization entries → staging `supertraining--verkhoshansky/claim--adaptive-reconstruction-vs-supercompensation.md`.
- Accumulation, transmutation, realization and prolonging entries → vault `research-papers/issurin-2016-benefits-and-limitations-...md`.
- Prolonging entry ↔ Ch1 `framework--training-stage-and-multi-peak-annual-cycle.md` (already one-way; its "special measures" line should link back).

## Overall verdict

**GO AFTER FIXES.** 0 GO, 12 FIX, 0 NO-GO.

- Every number in Tables 3.1, 3.3, 3.4, 3.5, 3.6, 3.8-3.14 and in the kayaker, Snell, Hooper (as the book tells it), Cardinale and triathlete passages matches the page.
- No `proven` rating is used. The case studies are correctly `untested`.
- Body-prose em dashes are gone.
- The taper and peaking entries are rated `supported`, which is the right ceiling. Neither duplicates a vault entry; the vault has no taper entry.

The failures are figure readings stamped "verified", source mechanisms merged or supplied, and the Ch1 labelling pattern (G1, G4) recurring.

Fixes, in priority order:

1. **Pre-competitive:** rewrite the Figure 3.7 description. The morning sport-specific key-workouts are the point of the design.
2. **Popov competition:** fix the title ("erased" is false: V-AT 1.57 → 1.63 → 1.60) and separate the hormonal and glycolytic (Volkov) chains.
3. **Prolonging mini-blocks:** fix the Example (no mini-block needed at 4-5 weeks; the 6-week arithmetic fails). Replace the invented mechanism with the author's "Apparently" hedge and state that no outcome data is given. Describe all Figure 3.12 patches. Add the "rigid and inflexible" caveat.
4. **Accumulation:** fix the Table 3.7 Options assignment, add the "three weeks or less" band, and fix the title.
5. **Transmutation:** re-ground or drop `contested` (recommend `supported`, with the baseline moved to When NOT). Add the Hooper primary-abstract discrepancy (n = 14, circular staleness definition, catecholamines added prediction). Credit the 5 bpm signal to its sources.
6. **Realization:** record the Figure 3.10 vs "69.3%" inconsistency and the Margaritis abstract discrepancy. Add the taper-mood sentence, the Fitz-Clarke tension and the G5 link.
7. **Sedykh:** fix the locator (idx 104 / p.93), add the pooled-sex confound, and fix the title scope.
8. **Popov aerobic:** add the author's glycolytic-exclusion mechanism, the Zatsiorsky strength trade-off, and the scope of the 24-h rule against Figure 3.4.
9. **In-season:** fix the Example against Figure 3.8 (Tue and Wed AM key lifts, Thu PM key practice, Fri off, Sunday game; shift one day for Saturday). Change "mesocycles" to "microcycles".
10. **Minor rows** (microcycle types, anaerobic glycolytic, construction heuristic): the labels and wording given in each row.
11. **Globals:** G1 labels on every Example and Population paragraph, G4 Issurin 2016 links, G5 supercompensation link, and correct `_book.md`'s "matched exactly" claim.

1	# Eric's method baseline (draft for Eric's review)
2	
3	Purpose: this is the step-1 baseline for Flint. It pulls every position, practice, and decision rule out of Eric's own 23-document corpus (Baylor Applied Performance playbook, protocols, assessment manual, professional writing, and HHPR 5355 graduate-course material) so that every future synthesis note comparing an outside source (Landon Evans, TB's Training Info, Old Bull, Harries RTP, SCN/Moyer, etc.) has something of Eric's own to compare against. Date: 2026-09-26.
4	
5	## Provenance note (read this before the bullets)
6	
7	Not all 23 documents are Eric's own words, and the two richest sources (the class transcripts) have a diarization problem. Read this once, then use these tags:
8	
9	- **Eric-authored, high confidence**: the two SportSmith articles, the Performance Playbook Development Plan, the Force Plate Testing V3 and Iso Seated Calf protocols, the Applied Performance Playbook (departmental document under his unit), and the HD ODSF metrics note (adopted practice, though the framework itself is Hawkin Dynamics' own).
10	- **Course slide decks (Week 1, Week 3, Class 4)**: co-branded to Ruf/Rash/Wenger on every title slide. Per `spring-2026-teaching.md`, Eric was the assigned instructor for the Feb. 5 and Feb. 12 sessions (Week 3 Lecture and Class 4 2026 respectively), so bullets from those two decks are marked **Explicit**. Week 1 (Jan. 22, "All") and Class 8/Lesson 8 (Mar. 19, Wenger's session) are marked **Inferred** — shared team material, not confirmed as Eric's individual position.
11	- **Both class transcripts (Class 1, Class 3) are diarized entirely under one Fireflies speaker label, "Chris Ruf," for every line, across 100+ minutes combined.** This is true even for Class 3 (Feb. 5), which the syllabus assigns solo to Rash. Fireflies likely defaulted to the meeting organizer's name rather than doing real per-speaker diarization. That means specific sentences in these transcripts cannot be confidently attributed to Rash vs. Ruf vs. Wenger. Bullets drawn from the transcripts are marked **Inferred**, with a citation note, even where the statement itself is a direct, confident, first-person claim in the text. Flint should treat these as "the HHPR 5355 teaching team's shared position, individual speaker unconfirmed" until Eric ratifies them.
12	  - **Confirmed by Eric, 2026-09-26:** HHPR 5355 is taught each spring by Chris Ruf, Eric and Mike Wenger. The lecture material is split among the three of them. This confirms the course is partly Eric's, but it cannot say who spoke a given transcript line. So transcript bullets stay tagged Inferred and read as **course team positions**. Each one becomes Eric's own only when he claims it, in review or in the interview.
13	- **Reference material, not Eric's position**: `intencurriculumn.md` is Jason Avedesian's (Clemson) authored curriculum end to end, used by the Development Plan as a benchmark, not as something Eric wrote or necessarily agrees with. The two Unit Goal Programming Standards documents are explicitly staff templates filled in (thinly) by Geyer and Skodinski, not Eric. The AP Assessment Manual V12 and the TechnologyTemplateSOP (TMG) have uncertain/likely-legacy authorship (see Tensions below) and are marked accordingly.
14	
15	Sections below use **Explicit** (the source states Eric holds this position, with confidence in authorship per the tiers above) and **Inferred** (implied by protocol design, shared course material, or transcript content with unconfirmed speaker attribution).
16	
17	---
18	
19	## Philosophy and decision principles
20	
21	- Applied Performance's stated mission is to "drive elite performance ... by leveraging science and technology through education and relationships," enabling the high-performance team to answer questions, ask better questions, and discover new ones — not to hand down answers unilaterally. **Explicit** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md p.6]
22	- The department's four operating principles are Athlete Monitoring and Analysis, Athlete Evaluation and Return-to-Performance, Performance Team Collaboration, and Research and Development. **Explicit** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md p.6]
23	- Institutional framing: "Prepare Champions for Life" across four pillars (academic, athletic, social, spiritual), operationalized through six "One Standard, One Accord" principles. **Explicit** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md pp.3-4]
24	- Data collection is judged on cost versus insight: "Data collection has a cost in time, athlete compliance, and staff attention. When the insight stops justifying that cost, it's time to stop collecting." **Explicit** [2026-02-19-sportsmith-6otb-er.md]
25	- A test can be scientifically valid and still be the wrong choice operationally: "The lesson wasn't about the test. It was about the infrastructure required to make a test useful ... even a valid test stops being valuable" without staff ownership and consistent collection. **Explicit** [2026-02-20-sportsmith-6otb-nordbord-er.md]
26	- "Inconsistent data from a good test is still bad data" — a test's validity doesn't rescue it if it can't be collected consistently at scale. **Explicit** [2026-02-20-sportsmith-6otb-nordbord-er.md]
27	- Reject ownership language ("my team," "my athletes"): the athlete's development is shared across every department that touches them, not owned by any one coach. **Inferred (transcript, speaker unconfirmed)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.5, "we got to get away from like the me and my"]
28	- Injury risk can be reduced, not eliminated, through sound programming, progression, and collaboration with Athletic Medicine — an explicit refusal to promise injury prevention. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.4]
29	- Be skeptical of social-media-driven training trends: a viral clip is "just a brief snapshot," stripped of the context that would tell you whether it's sound. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.3]
30	- Recovery has to be earned by training hard first; a culture of fear grew out of early GPS/load-monitoring work that pushed teams toward under-training in the name of "recovery." **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.9-10]
31	- "Knowledge from experience" as a stated operating value: safety first, keep things simple, teach basic movement skills and basic lifts before anything advanced, treat strength as the base, and require bodyweight competency before loaded work. **Inferred (transcript + Week 1 slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.4-5; week1-lecture.md p.12]
32	
33	## Department model and roles
34	
35	- Applied Performance operates inside the Baylor Athletics Health & Wellness department, alongside (not above or below) Athletics Performance, Athletic Medicine, Performance Nutrition, and Mental Health Services. **Explicit** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md pp.5-6]
36	- The athlete is described as the hub of a wheel, with every support function (academics, Athletic Medicine, nutrition, mental health, Applied Performance) as a spoke — no single discipline owns the athlete's development. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.5]

177	## Tensions and contradictions
178	
179	1. **The task's own premise doesn't fully hold.** Both class transcripts (Class 1 and Class 3) are diarized entirely under a single Fireflies speaker label, "Chris Ruf," for every line — including Class 3, which the Spring 2026 teaching schedule assigns solo to Rash (`spring-2026-teaching.md`: "Feb. 5 | Conditioning - Alactic-Aerobic | Rash"). Fireflies likely defaulted to the meeting organizer's name instead of doing real per-speaker diarization. This means roughly 30,000 words of the richest, most first-person material in this corpus cannot be confidently attributed to Rash specifically versus Ruf or Wenger. Every transcript-sourced bullet above is marked Inferred for this reason, even where the underlying statement is a confident, first-person claim.

181	2. **Department reporting model is not internally consistent.** The Playbook (p.6) frames Applied Performance as a peer discipline inside Health & Wellness that "enables" Athletics Performance, Athletic Medicine, Nutrition, and Mental Health to answer their own questions. But Week 1 course material lists "Applied Performance" as one of many training sub-categories nested under Athletic Performance itself (p.11), and the same transcript narration describes Rash's role as "helping program and plan the training" — a support-staff framing, not a peer-department framing. Which model actually governs day-to-day authority is not reconciled anywhere in these documents.
182	
183	3. **Coach's-eye-first versus objective-first is argued both ways.** The course material repeatedly argues that "you don't need a fancy test... you have to have a good coach's eye" and criticizes the GPS/load-monitoring era for breeding a fear-driven under-training culture. Eric's own SportSmith writing moves the opposite direction on daily monitoring specifically: he replaced subjective wellness surveys with objective force-plate mRSI because subjective self-report couldn't be trusted. Both share a skepticism of trendy or convenient data, but they land on opposite defaults (trust the trained eye vs. require an objective number) for the daily-monitoring question specifically.
184	
185	4. **The Assessment Manual (V12) reads as an older document than the current technology stack.** It builds its 1RM-estimation protocol around GymAware, and its CMJ description references a "contact mat" for jump height. The current Playbook technology stack and the Development Plan both center velocity-based training on Perch, not GymAware, and the current Force Plate Testing V3 protocol runs all CMJ variants exclusively on ForceDecks force plates, with no contact mat mentioned. This suggests the Assessment Manual predates the current VALD/Perch-centered stack and may be a legacy document rather than the currently operative protocol — worth confirming directly with Eric before treating any of its specifics as current practice.
186	
187	5. **Testing cueing instructions conflict across two protocol documents for the same test.** The Assessment Manual's CMJ instructions say explicitly: "Do not coach the strategy of jumping." The current Force Plate Testing V3 protocol gives testers specific verbal cues to give athletes during CMJ, squat-jump, and hop-test administration ("keep chest up," "land softly," "land stiff-legged on only the toes"). These may be reconcilable (safety/technique cues vs. jump-strategy cues are different things), but the two documents read differently on how much a tester should say out loud.
188	
189	6. **Two different anaerobic-threshold heart-rate methods appear back to back in the same slide deck without being reconciled.** One slide gives an age-based formula (max HR = 220-age for men, 226-age for women, threshold at ~85% of that), and the very next slides give a body-size-based table (big/medium/small athlete, ~165/170/175 bpm threshold) as the operational standard used elsewhere throughout the conditioning material. Which one is actually used day to day is not stated. [class-4-2026.md pp.27-29]
190	
191	7. **The Development Plan's own critique cuts against the corpus it's part of.** It states the current Baylor Playbook "has no educational component whatsoever" and reads "like a vendor product reference manual," even though Eric personally co-teaches a full graduate-level course covering much of the same material the Playbook is missing. The department's teaching capacity clearly exists; it just hasn't been captured back into the Playbook or a formal intern curriculum yet.
192	
193	8. **The Playbook's NordBord documentation has not caught up with practice.** The Playbook's Technology Overview and Workflows still document a full, unqualified, roster-style NordBord data-collection SOP. The SportSmith piece describes explicitly retiring roster-wide NordBord testing for football starting after January 2023, keeping it only for small, targeted return-to-play groups. The written SOP has not been updated to reflect that decision.
194	
195	9. **A personally-stated periodization preference is stated inside an unreliable-speaker transcript.** "For me personally, this is a more preferential model to use" (about undulating over linear periodization) is a strong, direct, first-person preference claim — but it comes from the same unreliably-diarized Class 1 transcript described in Tension 1, so it cannot be confirmed as Eric's own stated preference without his direct confirmation.
196	
197	10. **Older vs. current unit-goal templates show almost no adopted content.** The Geyer and Skodinski Unit Goal Programming Standards documents are staff-authored templates for individual sport programming philosophy; Geyer's is mostly filled in (periodization model, weekly split, KPI tests for softball), Skodinski's is nearly blank (just the section headers). Neither is attributed to Eric, and there's no equivalent document in this corpus showing Eric's own answers to the same template questions — a real gap if Flint wants Eric's own unit-goal-style programming philosophy in his own words.
198	
199	---
200	
201	## Named influences
202	
203	| Influence | What's credited to them | Where | Provenance |
204	|---|---|---|---|
205	| Al Vermeil (transcribed once as "Albert Meal") | Hierarchy of athletic development (work capacity → strength → power → speed → sport skill); described as the department's programming "compass" | class1-transcript.md pp.9-10, 18-19 | Course material, speaker unconfirmed |
206	| Dan Pfaff (transcribed as "Coach Path/Paf/Pabst") | The "coach's eye" ideal — biomechanical assessment purely by trained observation, illustrated with an anecdote about diagnosing a runner's spinal alignment from 50 meters away | class1-transcript.md pp.6-7 | Course material, speaker unconfirmed |
207	| Yuri Verkhoshansky | Principle of Dynamic Correspondence, for judging real exercise transfer | class1-transcript.md p.14; week1-lecture.md p.34 | Course material |
208	| Anatoly Bondarchuk (transcribed as "Bondurciu") | General prep / specific prep / specific development / competitive exercise taxonomy | class1-transcript.md p.16; week1-lecture.md p.36 | Course material |
209	| Johnny Parker, Al Miller, Rob Panariello (transcribed as "Panarillo") | Undulating/non-linear periodization model, described as personally preferred | class1-transcript.md pp.25-26; week1-lecture.md pp.59-63; lesson8summary.md #19 | Course material |
210	| Louis Simmons / Westside Barbell (via Zatsiorsky and Siff) | Conjugate/concurrent method: max effort, dynamic effort, repetitive effort | class1-transcript.md pp.26-27; week1-lecture.md pp.63-66 | Course material |
211	| A.S. Prilepin (transcribed once as "the Philippines chart") | Rep/set/intensity guide, used as the default across strength and power teaching | class1-transcript.md p.19; week1-lecture.md p.47; hhpr-5355-class-8-2026.md p.15 | Shared team material |
212	| Tracy Fober | "Use a barbell like a chisel, not a sledgehammer" — quality-first coaching maxim, cited from a 2019 Baylor AP clinic and her Instagram | class1-transcript.md p.21; week1-lecture.md p.46 | Course material |
213	| Stu McMillan | Four goals of strength training (produce force, absorb force, decrease injury chance, teach positional context) | lesson8summary.md #3; hhpr-5355-class-8-2026.md p.5 | Wenger's session (Mar. 19) |
214	| Fred Hatfield; JL Holdsworth | Strength/alignment aphorisms ("can't shoot a cannon out of a canoe"; "monster tires on a Prius with bad alignment") | hhpr-5355-class-8-2026.md p.4; lesson8summary.md #2 | Wenger's session |
215	| Joel Jamieson (*Ultimate MMA Conditioning*) | Recommended as the best practical resource on energy-system development methods | 2026-02-05-hp5355-class3-transcript.md pp.11-12; week3-lecture.md pp.49-50 | Eric's assigned session (transcript speaker unconfirmed; slides confirmed) |
216	| Jason Avedesian / Clemson Olympic Sports Science | Entire intern curriculum (force plates, GPS, force-velocity profiling, data hygiene, visualization, soft skills, research methods, injury risk, S&C) | intencurriculumn.md, all pages | Reference source, not Eric's voice — used by the Development Plan as a benchmark |
217	| Hawkin Dynamics | Output/Driver/Strategy/Fluffy (ODSF) metric-selection framework for force-plate reporting | hd-odsf-metrics.md | Vendor framework, adopted as practice |
218	| NSCA (*Essentials of Sport Science* / CPSS) | Textbook basis for the Clemson curriculum and for Baylor's own proposed intern curriculum | performance-playbook-development-plan.md Section 5 | Cited by Eric's own Development Plan |
219	| Zatsiorsky; Haff & Triplett; Parker/Miller/Panariello (*The System*) | Recommended HHPR 5355 course textbooks | week1-lecture.md p.4 | Course syllabus |
