13	
14	# Six Microcycle Types by Purpose and Load, With One-, Two-, and Three-Peak Weekly Load Waves
15	
16	**What it is** — Table 3.1 (PDF p. 88, printed p. 77; verified against the page image)
17	gives six microcycle types, each with a stated purpose, load level, design particular, and
18	duration range: **Adjustment** (initial adaptation to loads, medium load, gradual workload
19	increase, **5-7 days**); **Loading** (fitness development, substantial-high load, big/substantial
20	workloads, **5-9 days**); **Impact** (fitness development via extreme stimuli, very
21	high-extreme load, summation of extreme workloads, **4-7 days**); **Pre-competitive**
22	(immediate preparation for competition, medium load, tuning with event-specific means,
23	**5-7 days**, see [[framework--pre-competitive-microcycle-tuning]] for full detail);
24	**Competitive** (participation in competition, high-very high load, sport/event-specific
25	performance, **2-7 days**); **Restoration** (active recovery, low load, wide spectrum of
26	restorative means, **3-7 days**). Issurin notes the adjustment microcycle can shorten to
27	3-5 days mid-season (e.g., starting a new training stage or a camp), and the restoration
28	microcycle after camp or competition typically runs 3-4 days mid-season (PDF p. 88, printed
29	p. 77). Separately, Issurin describes load variation **within** a microcycle as a "wave-shape
30	design" using the 5-point load scale from [[framework--workout-load-classification-and-rpe-mapping]]:
31	Figure 3.1 (PDF p. 90, printed p. 79) shows one-, two-, and three-peak weekly load patterns
32	for single-workout-per-day microcycles. Two- and three-peak designs are described as "used
33	most widely" because they let athletes handle a relatively large weekly workload with reduced
34	excessive-fatigue risk; the one-peak design concentrates several developmental workouts for a
35	"more profound and stressful training response," a pattern reserved for "sufficiently
36	prepared high-performance athletes" and not for novices. For microcycles with two workouts
37	per day, Figure 3.2 (PDF p. 91, printed p. 80) gives a worked ten-workout example: two
38	development workouts open the week (first peak), two medium-load supporting workouts
39	provide restoration, then a three-session mini-block including two key-workouts forms the
40	second peak, with the week's final session usable as a time-trial or scrimmage.
41	
42	**Why it works** — Issurin frames the point-scale quantification (adapted from the 5-point
43	load scale) as serving three purposes: it lets coaches in non-measurable sports (sailing,
44	team/dual sports) express load numerically and visually; it lets athletes see and
45	consciously anticipate key-workouts and the restoration that follows load peaks
46	(a didactic use); and it lets whole microcycles be compared to each other for planning
47	purposes (PDF pp. 91-92, printed pp. 80-81). The peak/trough pattern itself follows the same
48	general logic as [[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]]: concentrating the
49	week's hardest sessions into one, two, or three peaks (rather than spreading maximal effort
50	evenly across every day) lets fatigue clear between peaks so each peak can still be
51	performed at a high standard.
52	
53	**When to apply** — Classifying a week's purpose before assigning workouts to it (is this
54	week meant to adjust athletes to new load, develop fitness, deliver an extreme stimulus, tune
55	for competition, compete, or actively recover), and then shaping that week's daily load curve
56	around one, two, or three peaks depending on athlete level and the week's targeted abilities.
57	**Inference, mapped to a college football calendar:** early fall camp days function like
58	Issurin's **adjustment** microcycle (medium load, gradual ramp, until two-a-days are
59	tolerated); the heaviest camp week(s) resemble the **impact** type (very high-extreme load,
60	short duration, 4-7 days, matching the "impact week" concept sometimes used informally in
61	strength-staff planning); the week of the season opener and each bowl-prep week function as
62	**pre-competitive** microcycles (see [[framework--pre-competitive-microcycle-tuning]]); a
63	normal in-season game week is Issurin's **competitive** microcycle in form (the whole week
64	organized around one **competition**, 2-7 days), though its internal training content is
65	closer to what [[framework--in-season-team-sport-mini-block-microcycle]] describes; and a bye
66	week or the week after a game before a short turnaround functions as a **restoration**
67	microcycle. **Eric's baseline** does not currently name these six categories explicitly, but
68	the general planning language ("a 'training week' does not have to equal 7 calendar days,"
69	`method-baseline.md`, "Periodization and programming," citing week1-lecture.md p.39) is
70	consistent with treating microcycle type, not just calendar week, as the planning unit.
71	
72	**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — The six-type table's specific duration ranges are
73	Issurin's own applied categorization; no citation or derivation is given for why, e.g., the
74	loading type is 5-9 days rather than some other range. **Inference:** none of the six types
75	or the one-/two-/three-peak wave figures are demonstrated on a team-sport example in this
76	section (that comes later, 3.1.7); the load-wave figures here are drawn from individual/dual
77	sport contexts, and the specific number-of-peaks guidance ("one-peak... not [for] novice and
78	less prepared athletes") is stated for individual-sport training loads, not validated for a
79	100+ player roster with heterogeneous training ages. The point-scale system inherits every
80	limitation already logged for the underlying RPE/restoration-time scale in
81	[[framework--workout-load-classification-and-rpe-mapping]] (subjective, no cited validation
82	of the specific cut-points).
83	
84	**Example** — A four-week fall-camp block could be read as adjustment (days 1-5, single
85	practices, medium load) into loading (days 6-14, one-a-days plus early two-a-days) into an
86	impact microcycle (the hardest stretch of two-a-days, 4-7 days) into a pre-competitive
87	microcycle in the week before the opener, each transition marked by a deliberate change in
88	purpose and load level, not just a generic "camp is getting harder" narrative.
89	
90	**Related** — [[framework--workout-load-classification-and-rpe-mapping]] (the 5-point scale
91	this section's point-quantification is built on), [[framework--pre-competitive-microcycle-tuning]],
92	[[framework--in-season-team-sport-mini-block-microcycle]],
93	[[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]],
94	[[framework--key-workout-and-key-exercise-concept]].

per day, Figure 3.2 (PDF p. 91, printed p. 80) gives a worked ten-workout example: two
development workouts open the week (first peak), two medium-load supporting workouts
provide restoration, then a three-session mini-block including two key-workouts forms the
second peak, with the week's final session usable as a time-trial or scrimmage.

**Why it works** — Issurin frames the point-scale quantification (adapted from the 5-point
load scale) as serving three purposes: it lets coaches in non-measurable sports (sailing,
team/dual sports) express load numerically and visually; it lets athletes see and
consciously anticipate key-workouts and the restoration that follows load peaks
(a didactic use); and it lets whole microcycles be compared to each other for planning
purposes (PDF pp. 91-92, printed pp. 80-81). The peak/trough pattern itself follows the same
general logic as [[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]]: concentrating the
week's hardest sessions into one, two, or three peaks (rather than spreading maximal effort
evenly across every day) lets fatigue clear between peaks so each peak can still be
performed at a high standard.

**When to apply** — Classifying a week's purpose before assigning workouts to it (is this
week meant to adjust athletes to new load, develop fitness, deliver an extreme stimulus, tune
for competition, compete, or actively recover), and then shaping that week's daily load curve
around one, two, or three peaks depending on athlete level and the week's targeted abilities.
**Inference, mapped to a college football calendar:** early fall camp days function like
Issurin's **adjustment** microcycle (medium load, gradual ramp, until two-a-days are
tolerated); the heaviest camp week(s) resemble the **impact** type (very high-extreme load,
short duration, 4-7 days, matching the "impact week" concept sometimes used informally in
strength-staff planning); the week of the season opener and each bowl-prep week function as
**pre-competitive** microcycles (see [[framework--pre-competitive-microcycle-tuning]]); a
normal in-season game week is Issurin's **competitive** microcycle in form (the whole week
organized around one **competition**, 2-7 days), though its internal training content is
closer to what [[framework--in-season-team-sport-mini-block-microcycle]] describes; and a bye
week or the week after a game before a short turnaround functions as a **restoration**
microcycle. **Eric's baseline** does not currently name these six categories explicitly, but
the general planning language ("a 'training week' does not have to equal 7 calendar days,"
`method-baseline.md`, "Periodization and programming," citing week1-lecture.md p.39) is
consistent with treating microcycle type, not just calendar week, as the planning unit.

**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — The six-type table's specific duration ranges are
Issurin's own applied categorization; no citation or derivation is given for why, e.g., the
loading type is 5-9 days rather than some other range. **Inference:** none of the six types
or the one-/two-/three-peak wave figures are demonstrated on a team-sport example in this
section (that comes later, 3.1.7); the load-wave figures here are drawn from individual/dual
sport contexts, and the specific number-of-peaks guidance ("one-peak... not [for] novice and
less prepared athletes") is stated for individual-sport training loads, not validated for a
100+ player roster with heterogeneous training ages. The point-scale system inherits every
limitation already logged for the underlying RPE/restoration-time scale in
[[framework--workout-load-classification-and-rpe-mapping]] (subjective, no cited validation
of the specific cut-points).

**Example** — A four-week fall-camp block could be read as adjustment (days 1-5, single
practices, medium load) into loading (days 6-14, one-a-days plus early two-a-days) into an
impact microcycle (the hardest stretch of two-a-days, 4-7 days) into a pre-competitive
microcycle in the week before the opener, each transition marked by a deliberate change in
purpose and load level, not just a generic "camp is getting harder" narrative.

this section's point-quantification is built on), [[framework--pre-competitive-microcycle-tuning]],
[[framework--in-season-team-sport-mini-block-microcycle]],
[[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]],

microcycle; (b) strength can be developed effectively through force accentuation inside

timing rule: strength work should not follow directly after exhaustive aerobic training,
because the testosterone/cortisol ratio needed for protein synthesis stays depressed for
"many hours" post-endurance-work (Viru, Karelson & Smirnova, 1992); **24 hours** of recovery,
with only low-level loads in between, is stated as the needed gap (PDF p. 95, printed p. 84,
citing Chesley et al., 1992 for protein-turnover persisting ≥24 hours post-resistance-work).

**Why it works** — Issurin's own stated mechanism for combining aerobic and strength work is
that concurrent aerobic stimulus improves oxidative support in the muscle mass strength

[[case-study--concurrent-training-interference-and-decay]]) that strength-built muscle mass

performance. The 24-hour strength-after-aerobic sequencing rule follows directly from the
testosterone/cortisol citation: an anabolic hormonal environment is a precondition for the
strength stimulus to "take," and that environment is temporarily suppressed right after

aerobic base and strength, and specifically the 24-hour strength-after-aerobic spacing rule

microcycle. **Inference:** for football specifically, this example argues against treating

metabolic and technical demands (continuous, cyclical, non-contact, highly technique-limited)
differ substantially from football; the specific finding that glycolytic training is nearly
absent in this microcycle should not be read as "football conditioning should minimize
glycolytic work"; Eric's baseline's own stated fall-camp priority stack treats glycolytic

25	imposes comparable fatigue on technique). Issurin gives specific lactate-based intensity

14	# Sedykh's Hammer-Throw Microcycle Puts Explosive Strength Only in Morning, Fresh-Athlete Sessions
15	
16	**What it is** — Issurin presents the eleven-workout microcycle of two-time Olympic champion
17	hammer thrower Yuri Sedykh (USSR), as reported by his coach (Bondarchuk, 1986) (PDF pp.
18	101-103, printed pp. 90-92, Table 3.4 and Figure 3.6). Four essential features: (a)
19	event-specific explosive-strength exercises (throwing different-weight hammers), the
20	top-priority target, appear **exclusively** in morning sessions and always in the **initial**
21	part of the workout, to use the athlete's most favorable physical state for the key-exercise;
22	(b) maximum-strength exercises (barbell snatch, half squats, good mornings), a supporting
23	role, are placed in five sessions: four separate evening sessions plus once in the second
24	part of a morning session; (c) additional explosive-strength work (standing jumps) appears
25	three times, but never when the athlete is in his best condition, i.e., placed after the
26	primary explosive work is already done; (d) restorative activity (basketball, swimming,
27	stretching) is built into the program, including on the day off. Issurin separately cites a
28	related mechanism study: Cardinale and Stone (2006) measured resting blood testosterone and
29	countermovement vertical jump in 70 elite athletes (48 men, 22 women; sprinters, handball,
30	volleyball, soccer) after a 10-hour fast and a rest day, finding a significant positive
31	relationship between testosterone and jump height (r = 0.61, p < 0.001) (PDF p. 103, printed
32	p. 92). Issurin's own stated implications from that study: athletes with relatively high
33	testosterone (either sex) have some inherited predisposition for explosive-strength
34	performance, and microcycle design for explosive-strength development should avoid excessive
35	fatigue, because fatigue suppresses testosterone and sharply reduces the training effect of
36	maximal-power exercises.

# Sedykh's Hammer-Throw Microcycle Puts Explosive Strength Only in Morning, Fresh-Athlete Sessions

**What it is** — Issurin presents the eleven-workout microcycle of two-time Olympic champion
hammer thrower Yuri Sedykh (USSR), as reported by his coach (Bondarchuk, 1986) (PDF pp.
101-103, printed pp. 90-92, Table 3.4 and Figure 3.6). Four essential features: (a)
event-specific explosive-strength exercises (throwing different-weight hammers), the
top-priority target, appear **exclusively** in morning sessions and always in the **initial**
part of the workout, to use the athlete's most favorable physical state for the key-exercise;
(b) maximum-strength exercises (barbell snatch, half squats, good mornings), a supporting
role, are placed in five sessions: four separate evening sessions plus once in the second
part of a morning session; (c) additional explosive-strength work (standing jumps) appears
three times, but never when the athlete is in his best condition, i.e., placed after the
primary explosive work is already done; (d) restorative activity (basketball, swimming,
stretching) is built into the program, including on the day off. Issurin separately cites a
related mechanism study: Cardinale and Stone (2006) measured resting blood testosterone and
countermovement vertical jump in 70 elite athletes (48 men, 22 women; sprinters, handball,
volleyball, soccer) after a 10-hour fast and a rest day, finding a significant positive
relationship between testosterone and jump height (r = 0.61, p < 0.001) (PDF p. 103, printed
p. 92). Issurin's own stated implications from that study: athletes with relatively high
testosterone (either sex) have some inherited predisposition for explosive-strength
performance, and microcycle design for explosive-strength development should avoid excessive
fatigue, because fatigue suppresses testosterone and sharply reduces the training effect of
maximal-power exercises.

**Why it works** — Issurin's stated mechanism (PDF pp. 103-104, printed pp. 92-93) is that
explosive strength depends on the sensitivity
and reactivity of the neuromuscular system, and excessive fatigue "disrupts the subtle
regulation of neural input and muscle contraction"; testosterone is named as the hormone
determining strength training's anabolic effect and as an index of induced physical stress
(Viru and Viru, 2000). **Inference:** the placement rule (explosive work only when fresh,
morning, first in the session) follows directly from this same logic already generalized in
[[heuristic--exercise-sequencing-by-fatigue-state]]: CNS-dependent, high-precision qualities
need a well-rested athlete, and this case study is simply that general rule applied to one
specific, historically documented program.

**When to apply** — As a concrete illustration of sequencing explosive/technical power work
at the very start of a session, before any fatigue-inducing supporting work, for athletes
whose primary target ability is explosive strength in a highly coordinated skill.
**Inference:** in football, this maps most directly to skill-position or specialist
explosive-power development (e.g., jump-training or Olympic-lift-variant work meant to
transfer to explosive movement): placing that work first in a session, before conditioning
or high-volume accessory work, mirrors Sedykh's morning-first placement of hammer throws.

**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — This is a single elite thrower's program from a single
coach's secondhand report (Bondarchuk, 1986), with no comparison athlete or outcome data
beyond the general BPC narrative already logged in
[[case-study--bondarchuk-hammer-throw-block-mesocycles]]: it illustrates a design principle,
not a validated dose-response result. **Inference:** hammer throw is an acyclic, single-effort,
highly technical power event with no contact and no in-competition fatigue accumulation across
a "game," unlike football; the specific workout counts, throw counts, and session splits in
Table 3.4 should not be copied as a template. The testosterone-jump correlation (Cardinale and
Stone, 2006) is cross-sectional and observational (r = 0.61 explains well under half the
variance in jump height): it identifies an association at one time point in rested athletes,
not a training intervention; it does not establish that raising testosterone directly causes
higher jump performance, only that they covary. Population also spans track, handball,
volleyball and soccer athletes of both sexes, not football specifically.

**Example** — A football skill player's Tuesday lift built around explosive-power development
(e.g., trap-bar jumps, medicine-ball throws) should be sequenced first in the session, on a day
following adequate rest, with any high-volume or fatiguing accessory work placed afterward,
not the reverse.

**Related** — [[heuristic--exercise-sequencing-by-fatigue-state]],
[[case-study--bondarchuk-hammer-throw-block-mesocycles]],
[[framework--key-workout-and-key-exercise-concept]].

14	# The Pre-Competitive Microcycle: Cut Volume Hard, Raise Maximal-Speed and Sport-Specific Work, Keep Frequency
15	
16	**What it is** — The pre-competitive microcycle forms the content of the realization
17	mesocycle (see [[framework--realization-mesocycle-taper-prescription]]) and is also called the
18	taper at the microcycle level (PDF pp. 104-105, printed pp. 93-94; verified against page
19	images). It must satisfy three demands (PDF p. 104, printed p. 93): sport-specific
20	exercises/tasks that simulate the forthcoming competition and build mental readiness and
21	toughness; development of maximal speed/power and sport-specific quickness; and full (or
22	partial) restoration after the preceding transmutation mesocycle's fatiguing workloads. Table
23	3.5 (PDF p. 105, printed p. 94, verified against page image) gives seven prescriptive
24	characteristics: **workload volume**, substantially reduced, to create conditions for full
25	recovery; **volume of intense exercises specifically**, substantially reduced versus the
26	prior mesocycle, so total drill volume falls but quality rises; **contribution of maximum
27	speed/power exercises**, substantially **increased** (well-rested athletes respond better to
28	maximal-speed drills, and maximal-speed training residuals are the shortest of any ability, per
29	[[claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]]); **contribution of
30	sport-specific tasks**, substantially increased (simulative tasks improve adaptation to
31	expected competitive stressors); **workout frequency**, usually kept **similar** to the
32	previous mesocycle (subdividing the same total work into more, smaller portions raises
33	quality per session even as volume falls); **organization**, a rational mix of group,
34	individual and mixed workouts, weighted somewhat more toward individual work than usual, so
35	athletes can attend to personal technical detail and coach rapport; **restoration**,
36	deliberately favorable conditions and an increased volume of restorative exercises/workouts,
37	since athletes have more free time and motivation to use it. Issurin states that in qualified
38	athletes, especially during a pre-competitive training camp, maintaining frequency in practice
39	means **eight to ten workouts per week** even as volume per workout drops (PDF p. 106, printed
40	p. 95). Workout timing should match the expected competition's daily biological-rhythm window
41	(example given: Olympic canoe-kayak/rowing regattas run only in the morning, so pre-Olympic
42	training is scheduled to place peak-effort sessions at that same morning time, PDF p. 107,
43	printed p. 96). Figure 3.7 (PDF p. 108, printed p. 97) gives a worked chart for a
44	morning-peak-performance pre-competitive microcycle, alternating maximum-strength/technique
45	mornings with sport-specific-simulation/alactic afternoons, moving toward heavier
46	sport-specific-simulation and explosive-strength content later in the week. On strength work
47	specifically, Issurin notes a real disagreement in the field: many athletes (particularly
48	swimmers, per Platonov & Fesenko, 1990, and also reported among volleyball and tennis players)
49	report high-resistance work pre-competition degrades fine technical skill, arguing for
50	reducing or excluding it; but sport-specific maximal/explosive strength work is also argued to
51	maintain the technical force component (Bompa & Carrera, 2003) and to prevent uncontrolled,
52	stress-hormone-driven muscle-mass loss pre-competition (PDF p. 108, printed p. 97).
53	
54	**Why it works** — Reduced total load is stated as the "principal condition" for reaching
55	supercompensation before competition (PDF p. 106, printed p. 95); the two things this
56	recovered state is then spent on, maximal-speed drills and sport-specific simulation, are
57	each chosen because their quality specifically depends on a well-rested nervous system and
58	energy-resource availability (maximal speed) or on the athlete's capacity to fully attend to
59	technical/tactical detail under simulated competitive stress (sport-specific tasks). Keeping
60	frequency similar while cutting volume is explicitly a quality lever, not a rest lever: more,
61	shorter, higher-quality sessions rather than fewer long ones.
62	
63	**When to apply — Inference, mapped to a college football calendar** — **Bowl prep:** the
64	week(s) immediately before a bowl game map most directly onto this framework: cut total
65	practice/lift volume hard, hold practice frequency roughly where it has been, shift the
66	practice mix toward maximal-speed/explosive work and heavy game-plan (sport-specific)
67	simulation, and weight walkthroughs/individual work more than a normal week. **In-season
68	tuning week:** the standard in-season game week already functions as a compressed version of
69	this pattern (practice volume tapers toward the game, Thursday/Friday sessions shift toward
70	walkthrough-intensity techno-tactical work); see
71	[[framework--in-season-team-sport-mini-block-microcycle]] for the specific team-sport
72	adaptation Issurin gives later in this chapter. **Season opener after fall camp:** the final
73	camp week before the opener is a pre-competitive microcycle relative to the whole camp block:
74	volume should come down from camp peak even though frequency (practice count) may stay similar.
75	The strength-during-taper disagreement Issurin reports (reduce high-resistance work vs. keep
76	sport-specific strength to protect force and prevent hormone-driven muscle loss) is directly
77	relevant to the recurring question of whether to lift heavy in bowl-prep week; this text does
78	not resolve it and presents both positions as live in the field. **Eric's baseline** gives no
79	session-frequency rule for a taper anywhere in `method-baseline.md`; the closest material is
80	the general in-season rule "maintain intensity, reduce volume" (`method-baseline.md`, "Strength
81	and power," citing `01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md` pp.20-21), which agrees directionally
82	(reduce volume, don't reduce intensity/speed work) but does not specify a frequency-holding
83	rule, an eight-to-ten-sessions-per-week figure, or an explicit sport-specific-task ramp; this
84	entry supplies that missing numeric structure, not something already adopted.
85	
86	**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — Every numeric particular in Table 3.5 (frequency held at
87	8-10/week, "substantially reduced/increased" volume and speed contributions) is Issurin's own
88	applied synthesis with no cited dose-response study behind the specific numbers; he
89	acknowledges directly that "many contradictions exist regarding workout duration and frequency
90	of high intensity exercises" in the pre-competitive/taper literature generally (PDF p. 105,
91	printed p. 94, citing Kubukeli et al., 2002). **Population caveat:** the worked example
92	(Figure 3.7) and both named case examples (Olympic canoe-kayak/rowing morning scheduling;
93	swimmer/volleyball/tennis strength-reduction reports) are individual, dual, or non-contact
94	sports; none address a 100+ player roster with heterogeneous individual readiness, a fixed
95	practice-week structure set partly by NCAA rules, or the additional load of team walkthroughs
96	and special-teams reps that a football pre-competitive week must still include. The
97	"8-10 workouts per week" frequency figure assumes an individual/dual-sport training camp
98	structure and should not be read as a literal session-count target for a football bowl-prep
99	week. Issurin does not address game-week travel, opponent scouting load, or academic-calendar
100	constraints anywhere in this framework.
101	
102	**Example** — A bowl-prep week could hold practice count similar to a normal in-season week
103	while cutting total practice/lift volume substantially, shifting a larger share of practice
104	time to explosive/speed work and full-speed game-plan simulation than a mid-season week would
105	carry, and deliberately expanding individual position-group time (film, technique correction)
106	relative to full-team periods, while treating the "how much to lift" question as an open
107	disagreement the source itself does not resolve, not a settled rule.
108	
109	**Related** — [[framework--realization-mesocycle-taper-prescription]],
110	[[framework--in-season-team-sport-mini-block-microcycle]],
111	[[claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]],
112	[[framework--microcycle-types-and-load-wave-design]],
113	[[supertraining--verkhoshansky/framework--fitness-fatigue-modeling-and-taper-timing]] (staging).

14	# A Two-Mini-Block Weekly Structure for In-Season Team Sports, Naming American Football Directly
15	
16	**What it is** — Issurin addresses the specific constraint that team and dual sports (he
17	names **soccer, American football, rugby, volleyball** explicitly) run a 20-35 week season
18	where "the possibility of inserting highly concentrated training blocks is very limited"
19	(PDF pp. 108-109, printed pp. 97-98). He cites Fleck and Kraemer (1997): players typically
20	maintain strength near pre-season levels for 14-16 weeks, after which strength variables
21	decrease dramatically. Because the usual one-week gap between games is too short to work
22	effectively on every training target (metabolic conditioning, maximal/explosive strength,
23	injury prevention, techno-tactical skill, game-specific endurance, active restoration) at once,
24	Issurin proposes adapting three BPC approaches at the *week* level: high concentration of
25	specialized workloads within **mini-blocks**, separating mini-blocks by training modality, and
26	determining **key-workouts** within each mini-block. The worked example (Figure 3.8, PDF p.
27	109, printed p. 98, "based on Baker, 2001," a real cited source, not an uncited synthesis)
28	splits a standard Monday-Sunday week into two mini-blocks. **Mini-block 1 (Monday-Wednesday)**
29	targets sport-specific maximal and explosive strength as the dominant training aim: it opens
30	Monday with an active-recovery session (medium/low load, aerobic and general conditioning),
31	then delivers the strength emphasis across **two key-workouts**, combined with a medium-load
32	team practice (Tuesday afternoon) and a conditioning-restorative workout (Wednesday afternoon).
33	This sequencing leaves **28-30 hours of recovery** after the strength key-workouts before
34	mini-block 2 begins, to let the anabolic/restorative process run before the next demand.
35	**Mini-block 2 (Thursday-Saturday)** targets sport-specific team practice and immediate game
36	preparation: it includes two obligatory team practices, one before the day off (intended to
37	deliver a pronounced game-specific stimulus) and a second, load-restricted session immediately
38	before the game itself (mostly techno-tactical drills tied to the specific forthcoming
39	opponent). Issurin notes some highly motivated teams skip the day off and add an optional
40	Friday-morning conditioning or techno-tactical session instead, trading recovery time for
41	extra preparation; he states the tradeoff explicitly without endorsing either choice. The
42	chart gives priority to maximal-strength development over explosive-type work within the week,
43	which Issurin explains as protecting "somatic, functional and anabolic status," while noting a
44	cited counter-example (Newton et al., 2006) of sequencing classic high-resistance training with
45	ballistic explosive-type mesocycles to enhance jump performance instead.
46	
47	**Why it works** — The mini-block structure is this chapter's direct answer to the constraint
48	stated in [[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]] (BPC needs concentrated,
49	sequenced blocks) meeting the constraint that team sports cannot suspend competition long
50	enough to run full-length accumulation/transmutation/realization mesocycles
51	(see [[framework--accumulation-mesocycle-duration-and-monitoring]] and
52	[[framework--transmutation-mesocycle-duration-and-overtraining-monitoring]] for what those
53	normally require in duration). Splitting the week itself into two purpose-specific mini-blocks,
54	each with its own key-workouts, is Issurin's way of keeping some of BPC's concentration
55	benefit even though the underlying block can only be one week long, not several.
56	
57	**When to apply — this is the entry most directly answering the in-season half of the
58	strength-and-conditioning miss-log's "peaking phase structure for collegiate football" gap
59	(logged 2026-09-03)** — Issurin explicitly names American football as a sport this structure
60	is meant for. **Eric's baseline's** in-season rule, "maintain intensity, reduce volume"
61	(`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power," citing `01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md`
62	pp.20-21), is compatible with and gets a concrete weekly shape from this framework: the
63	early-week mini-block is where intensity (maximal/explosive strength) gets its two key-workouts,
64	while the late-week mini-block is deliberately techno-tactical and load-restricted heading into
65	the game, which *is* the volume reduction the baseline rule calls for. The 28-30 hour recovery
66	window between the strength mini-block and the practice-heavy mini-block gives a specific,
67	citable number for how much gap a college program might target between its heaviest in-season
68	lift and the next high-intensity team session.
69

71	one cited source, Baker (2001), a study of professional and college-aged rugby league players'

# A Two-Mini-Block Weekly Structure for In-Season Team Sports, Naming American Football Directly

**What it is** — Issurin addresses the specific constraint that team and dual sports (he
names **soccer, American football, rugby, volleyball** explicitly) run a 20-35 week season
where "the possibility of inserting highly concentrated training blocks is very limited"
(PDF pp. 108-109, printed pp. 97-98). He cites Fleck and Kraemer (1997): players typically
maintain strength near pre-season levels for 14-16 weeks, after which strength variables
decrease dramatically. Because the usual one-week gap between games is too short to work
effectively on every training target (metabolic conditioning, maximal/explosive strength,
injury prevention, techno-tactical skill, game-specific endurance, active restoration) at once,
Issurin proposes adapting three BPC approaches at the *week* level: high concentration of
specialized workloads within **mini-blocks**, separating mini-blocks by training modality, and
determining **key-workouts** within each mini-block. The worked example (Figure 3.8, PDF p.
109, printed p. 98, "based on Baker, 2001," a real cited source, not an uncited synthesis)
splits a standard Monday-Sunday week into two mini-blocks. **Mini-block 1 (Monday-Wednesday)**
targets sport-specific maximal and explosive strength as the dominant training aim: it opens
Monday with an active-recovery session (medium/low load, aerobic and general conditioning),
then delivers the strength emphasis across **two key-workouts**, combined with a medium-load
team practice (Tuesday afternoon) and a conditioning-restorative workout (Wednesday afternoon).
This sequencing leaves **28-30 hours of recovery** after the strength key-workouts before
mini-block 2 begins, to let the anabolic/restorative process run before the next demand.
**Mini-block 2 (Thursday-Saturday)** targets sport-specific team practice and immediate game
preparation: it includes two obligatory team practices, one before the day off (intended to
deliver a pronounced game-specific stimulus) and a second, load-restricted session immediately
before the game itself (mostly techno-tactical drills tied to the specific forthcoming
opponent). Issurin notes some highly motivated teams skip the day off and add an optional
Friday-morning conditioning or techno-tactical session instead, trading recovery time for
extra preparation; he states the tradeoff explicitly without endorsing either choice. The
chart gives priority to maximal-strength development over explosive-type work within the week,
which Issurin explains as protecting "somatic, functional and anabolic status," while noting a
cited counter-example (Newton et al., 2006) of sequencing classic high-resistance training with
ballistic explosive-type mesocycles to enhance jump performance instead.

**Why it works** — The mini-block structure is this chapter's direct answer to the constraint
stated in [[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]] (BPC needs concentrated,
sequenced blocks) meeting the constraint that team sports cannot suspend competition long
enough to run full-length accumulation/transmutation/realization mesocycles
(see [[framework--accumulation-mesocycle-duration-and-monitoring]] and
[[framework--transmutation-mesocycle-duration-and-overtraining-monitoring]] for what those
normally require in duration). Splitting the week itself into two purpose-specific mini-blocks,
each with its own key-workouts, is Issurin's way of keeping some of BPC's concentration
benefit even though the underlying block can only be one week long, not several.

**When to apply — this is the entry most directly answering the in-season half of the
strength-and-conditioning miss-log's "peaking phase structure for collegiate football" gap
(logged 2026-09-03)** — Issurin explicitly names American football as a sport this structure
is meant for. **Eric's baseline's** in-season rule, "maintain intensity, reduce volume"
(`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power," citing `01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md`
pp.20-21), is compatible with and gets a concrete weekly shape from this framework: the
early-week mini-block is where intensity (maximal/explosive strength) gets its two key-workouts,
while the late-week mini-block is deliberately techno-tactical and load-restricted heading into
the game, which *is* the volume reduction the baseline rule calls for. The 28-30 hour recovery
window between the strength mini-block and the practice-heavy mini-block gives a specific,
citable number for how much gap a college program might target between its heaviest in-season
lift and the next high-intensity team session.

**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — The specific day-by-day chart (Figure 3.8) is built from
one cited source, Baker (2001), a study of professional and college-aged rugby league players'
in-season concurrent training: a real, checkable citation, but a single study in rugby league,
a sport with a different weekly game/practice rhythm than college football, which layers
additional constraints (NCAA-mandated practice-time limits, travel, and a Saturday-only game
schedule rather than rugby league's varying weekly structure). **Population caveat:** none of
this section's evidence comes from American football itself; Issurin lists
football alongside soccer, rugby, and volleyball as sports the *problem* applies to, but the
worked example and its supporting citation are rugby-specific. **Inference:** the specific
"two key-workouts, 28-30 hours recovery" prescription should be treated as a structural
template to adapt to football's own practice-count and padded/unpadded-practice rules, not a
ready-made in-season lift schedule. Issurin gives no guidance here for bye weeks, short
(Thursday-game) weeks, or the postseason gap before a bowl game; those fall outside this
weekly-cycle framework and are closer to the pre-competitive/realization material in
[[framework--pre-competitive-microcycle-tuning]] and
[[framework--prolonging-residual-effects-with-mini-blocks]].

**Example** — A Baylor in-season week could place the two heaviest strength key-workouts on
Monday and Tuesday (following a Monday active-recovery/conditioning opener), hold Wednesday as
a conditioning-restorative bridge, then shift Thursday-Saturday entirely to team practice and
game-specific techno-tactical work, with the Friday or Saturday walkthrough load-restricted and
opponent-specific, and checking that the strength work and the first hard team practice of
mini-block 2 are separated by at least a full day, per the 28-30 hour figure.

14	# Build a Microcycle Key-Workouts First: A Six-Step Sequence and Five Design Rules
15	
16	**What it is** — Issurin gives a six-step operational sequence for compiling a training
17	microcycle (Table 3.6, PDF p. 111, printed p. 100): (1) determine dominant and secondary
18	training modalities, based on the annual plan and the current mesocycle's specificity; (2)
19	determine, place and compile **key-workouts** (see
20	[[framework--key-workout-and-key-exercise-concept]]), which carry the main development
21	impact; (3) determine restorative workouts and restorative "windows," to facilitate the
22	key-workouts and prevent excess fatigue; (4) determine, place and compile other
23	developmental/supportive workouts, paying special attention to how preceding workouts affect
24	sensitivity to subsequent ones; (5) select monitoring means for the targeted abilities and
25	functions; (6) plan special events (psychologist, physician, team meeting, etc.). Alongside
26	this sequence, Issurin states five general design rules (PDF p. 112, printed p. 101):
27	**first**, key-workout priority: once targeted abilities are defined, design should
28	start from the key-workouts, not fill them in last; **second**, arrangement around
29	key-workouts: the preceding session affects the athlete's sensitivity to the key-workout's
30	stimulus, while the following session determines fatigue accumulation and restoration, so both
31	neighbors must be chosen deliberately; **third**, sharing restorative means: restorative
32	workouts, restorative exercises (low-intensity aerobic work, stretching, relaxation, shaking,
33	breathing) and restorative procedures (massage, sauna, hydro/physiotherapy, mental training)
34	are "indispensable" and must be expertly planned into every microcycle, not treated as
35	optional filler; **fourth**, workload initiation and peaks: a day off lowers readiness for
36	high workloads, so the first session after a day off should **not** be a key-workout; the
37	number and placement of key-workouts is what determines whether the week is a one-, two-, or
38	three-peak design (see [[framework--microcycle-types-and-load-wave-design]]); **fifth**,
39	monitoring: key-workout execution data (achievement level, technical quality, HR, blood
40	lactate, RPE) is the single best indicator of an athlete's current state.
41	
42	**Why it works** — This is a process heuristic, not a physiological mechanism: Issurin's
43	stated rationale is that once the microcycle's actual development stimulus (the key-workouts)
44	is fixed, every other design decision (what precedes it, what follows it, how restoration is
45	distributed) exists to protect that stimulus's quality and manage the fatigue it produces.
46	Designing "everything else first, then slotting in the hard part" risks the key-workout landing
47	on a fatigued or under-prepared athlete.
48	
49	**When to apply** — As a checklist when building or auditing any microcycle: has the dominant
50	modality been named before workouts were scheduled; are the key-workouts placed away from the
51	first session after a day off; is there a planned restorative window around each key-workout;
52	and is monitoring tied specifically to key-workout performance rather than spread evenly across
53	every session. Useful as a coach-facing planning template independent of sport.
54	
55	**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — This is Issurin's own applied synthesis of BPC design
56	logic; no citation or comparative study is given for the six-step sequence or the five rules
57	themselves. Treat them as a structured practitioner heuristic, not an experimentally
58	validated planning method. **Inference:** the sequence assumes a coach already has a clear
59	single dominant-and-secondary modality assignment for the week (step 1); it gives no guidance
60	for a team-sport week that must simultaneously serve several position groups with different
61	dominant needs on the same day, a common real constraint in football that this chapter's
62	narrower single-athlete/single-event examples elsewhere do not have to solve.
63	
64	**Example** — Before finalizing a week's training plan, a coach could walk the six steps in
65	order: name this week's dominant ability, place its key-workouts (never as the first session
66	after a day off), build restorative windows around them, fill in supporting sessions with an
67	eye to how each affects the next, pick 2-3 monitoring indicators tied to the key-workouts, and
68	only then schedule any non-training events.
69	
70	**Related** — [[framework--key-workout-and-key-exercise-concept]],
71	[[framework--microcycle-types-and-load-wave-design]],
72	[[heuristic--exercise-sequencing-by-fatigue-state]].

# Build a Microcycle Key-Workouts First: A Six-Step Sequence and Five Design Rules

**What it is** — Issurin gives a six-step operational sequence for compiling a training
microcycle (Table 3.6, PDF p. 111, printed p. 100): (1) determine dominant and secondary
training modalities, based on the annual plan and the current mesocycle's specificity; (2)
determine, place and compile **key-workouts** (see
[[framework--key-workout-and-key-exercise-concept]]), which carry the main development
impact; (3) determine restorative workouts and restorative "windows," to facilitate the
key-workouts and prevent excess fatigue; (4) determine, place and compile other
developmental/supportive workouts, paying special attention to how preceding workouts affect
sensitivity to subsequent ones; (5) select monitoring means for the targeted abilities and
functions; (6) plan special events (psychologist, physician, team meeting, etc.). Alongside
this sequence, Issurin states five general design rules (PDF p. 112, printed p. 101):
**first**, key-workout priority: once targeted abilities are defined, design should
start from the key-workouts, not fill them in last; **second**, arrangement around
key-workouts: the preceding session affects the athlete's sensitivity to the key-workout's
stimulus, while the following session determines fatigue accumulation and restoration, so both
neighbors must be chosen deliberately; **third**, sharing restorative means: restorative
workouts, restorative exercises (low-intensity aerobic work, stretching, relaxation, shaking,
breathing) and restorative procedures (massage, sauna, hydro/physiotherapy, mental training)
are "indispensable" and must be expertly planned into every microcycle, not treated as
optional filler; **fourth**, workload initiation and peaks: a day off lowers readiness for
high workloads, so the first session after a day off should **not** be a key-workout; the
number and placement of key-workouts is what determines whether the week is a one-, two-, or
three-peak design (see [[framework--microcycle-types-and-load-wave-design]]); **fifth**,
monitoring: key-workout execution data (achievement level, technical quality, HR, blood
lactate, RPE) is the single best indicator of an athlete's current state.

**Why it works** — This is a process heuristic, not a physiological mechanism: Issurin's
stated rationale is that once the microcycle's actual development stimulus (the key-workouts)
is fixed, every other design decision (what precedes it, what follows it, how restoration is
distributed) exists to protect that stimulus's quality and manage the fatigue it produces.
Designing "everything else first, then slotting in the hard part" risks the key-workout landing
on a fatigued or under-prepared athlete.

**When to apply** — As a checklist when building or auditing any microcycle: has the dominant
modality been named before workouts were scheduled; are the key-workouts placed away from the
first session after a day off; is there a planned restorative window around each key-workout;
and is monitoring tied specifically to key-workout performance rather than spread evenly across
every session. Useful as a coach-facing planning template independent of sport.

**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — This is Issurin's own applied synthesis of BPC design
logic; no citation or comparative study is given for the six-step sequence or the five rules
themselves. Treat them as a structured practitioner heuristic, not an experimentally
validated planning method. **Inference:** the sequence assumes a coach already has a clear
single dominant-and-secondary modality assignment for the week (step 1); it gives no guidance
for a team-sport week that must simultaneously serve several position groups with different
dominant needs on the same day, a common real constraint in football that this chapter's
narrower single-athlete/single-event examples elsewhere do not have to solve.

**Example** — Before finalizing a week's training plan, a coach could walk the six steps in
order: name this week's dominant ability, place its key-workouts (never as the first session
after a day off), build restorative windows around them, fill in supporting sessions with an
eye to how each affects the next, pick 2-3 monitoring indicators tied to the key-workouts, and
only then schedule any non-training events.

14	# Accumulation Mesocycle: 3-6 Weeks Early, Down to 10-14 Days Late-Season, With Diminishing Weekly Returns
15	
16	**What it is** — This is the full prescriptive detail behind the accumulation block first
17	introduced conceptually in [[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]]
18	(Ch. 1). Issurin gives duration as a function of two competing factors (PDF pp. 113-115,
19	printed pp. 102-104): the time needed for a real cumulative training effect in the targeted
20	basic abilities, aerobic endurance and maximal strength, both requiring "profound morphological
21	and even organic changes," versus the time limit the competition calendar allows. He cites a
22	supporting case study: eight highly qualified female kayakers, monitored over a **20-week**
23	program of high-resistance training (**4-5 hr/week**) aimed at maximal strength and aerobic
24	endurance, tracked via maximal isometric force in kayak-specific positions (Figure 3.9, PDF p.
25	114, printed p. 103, based on Sharobajko, 1984). Strength gain and weekly improvement rate fell
26	sharply over time: the first 3 weeks produced a 5.9% average gain (1.93%/week improvement
27	rate); the next 3 weeks added only 1.6% more (0.53%/week); the remaining 14 weeks added only
28	0.25% and then 0.13% per week. Issurin's stated conclusion: the fitness program was "very
29	effective at the beginning, reasonably effective through the first six weeks, and had only a
30	minor effect for the next 14 weeks," directly supporting BPC's case for shorter, higher-turnover
31	blocks over long, continuous ones (citing the same general adaptive-decline concept in
32	Bouchard, 1986, as applying to aerobic-endurance programs too). Based on this, Issurin sets the
33	following duration bands (PDF p. 115, printed p. 104): **up to six weeks** when deeper
34	physiological change is the goal (typically early season, when athletes are less
35	calendar-constrained); **three-four weeks** at mid-season, once important-competition timing
36	starts to dictate mesocycle sequencing; **10-14 days** at season's end, when important
37	competitions come at short intervals. Content is structured by sequencing microcycle types
38	(Table 3.7, PDF p. 116, printed p. 105): the **initial** part uses a restoration microcycle
39	(if starting a new training stage, not needed after a transition period) followed by an
40	adjustment microcycle (can be shorter than a week); the **mid-and-end** part is built from
41	loading microcycles, whose count sets the mesocycle's total length, with optional impact and/or
42	restoration microcycles inserted (a restorative microcycle, usually 3-6 days, can go
43	mid-mesocycle, or immediately after an impact microcycle before the next loading microcycle).
44	General load-shape rule: increase load gradually at the start, hold maximal load in the middle,
45	and reduce load at the end so the next mesocycle (transmutation) begins without excess fatigue;
46	a 3-4 day restorative microcycle can be inserted near the end of accumulation for this purpose.
47	Monitoring (Table 3.8, PDF p. 117, printed p. 106; verified against page image) tracks three
48	categories: **workload performance** (total weekly mileage, total sport-specific reps/week,
49	key-workout outcomes, each compared actual-vs-planned, week-to-week, and across the season);
50	**targeted (basic) abilities** (time-trial results, free-weight-trial results, average
51	key-workout results, using "appropriate valid tests"); and **training responses** (resting
52	heart rate, blood urea and CPK, body mass/muscle mass/fat component, blood lactate after
53	trials). Anthropometric change is flagged as a specific, useful side-outcome to track (strength
54	training raises muscle mass; aerobic training reduces fat component), especially relevant in
55	weight-category or leanness-sensitive sports.
56	
57	**Why it works** — The kayaker case study is offered as direct evidence for the general
58	biological principle that "the adaptive response induced by long-term training declines with
59	time" (Bouchard, 1986): diminishing returns set in within weeks, not months, for a fixed
60	training emphasis, which is the physiological argument for keeping each mesocycle-block short
61	and switching emphasis rather than running one long undifferentiated program.
62	
63	**When to apply — Inference, mapped to a college football calendar** — **Fall camp** functions
64	as a short accumulation mesocycle at the low end of Issurin's range (closer to the 10-14 day
65	figure, or the 3-4 week figure if camp's aerobic/strength-base emphasis is counted from
66	voluntary summer conditioning): given the diminishing-returns pattern in the kayaker case
67	(most of a strength/aerobic gain arrives in the first 3-6 weeks), a multi-month, undifferentiated
68	summer conditioning block is exactly the pattern this framework argues against; a shorter,
69	concentrated base-building window, followed by a shift to more specific work, is the BPC
70	alternative. **The gap between the last regular-season/conference-championship game and a bowl
71	game** (commonly roughly 3-5 weeks for many programs) is long enough to support a short
72	accumulation mesocycle (10-14 to 20-25 days, matching both this section's end-of-season figure
73	and the mini-block interval used later in [[framework--prolonging-residual-effects-with-mini-blocks]])
74	if the goal is to rebuild any basic-ability deterioration accumulated over a long season before
75	shifting into a bowl-specific transmutation/realization sequence.
76	
77	**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — The kayaker case study is a single unpublished thesis
78	(Sharobajko, 1984, a Ph.D. dissertation, Moscow All-Union Research Sport Institute), n = 8,
79	female kayakers, with no control group not receiving the same 20-week program; it demonstrates
80	a within-group improvement-rate curve, not a controlled comparison against an alternative
81	mesocycle length. **Population caveat:** this is Issurin's own book-wide pattern: the
82	accumulation-duration guidance and its supporting evidence are drawn from individual/endurance
83	Olympic sports (kayaking) tracking isometric strength and presumably aerobic markers, not from
84	any team-contact-sport population; football's basic-ability profile (short-duration high-force
85	efforts, position-specific demands, large roster with heterogeneous training age) is not
86	represented in this evidence base at all. The specific duration bands (six weeks / 3-4 weeks /
87	10-14 days) are Issurin's own applied judgment, not derived from a stated formula connecting
88	them to the kayaker data's exact decay curve.
89	
90	**Example** — A 3-4 week early-summer strength-aerobic emphasis block, monitored against
91	Table 3.8's indicators (weekly key-lift totals, a repeated time-trial or aerobic test, resting
92	HR trend, body composition), gives a coach a citable structure for when to expect most of a
93	block's gain to already have happened (roughly the first half of the block, per the kayaker
94	curve) and when continuing the same emphasis is likely yielding only marginal further return.
95	
96	**Related** — [[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]],
97	[[claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]],
98	[[framework--transmutation-mesocycle-duration-and-overtraining-monitoring]],
99	[[case-study--popov-aerobic-strength-microcycle]],
100	[[periodization--bompa/framework--three-training-effects]].

key-workout results, using "appropriate valid tests"); and **training responses** (resting
heart rate, blood urea and CPK, body mass/muscle mass/fat component, blood lactate after
trials). Anthropometric change is flagged as a specific, useful side-outcome to track (strength
training raises muscle mass; aerobic training reduces fat component), especially relevant in
weight-category or leanness-sensitive sports.

**Why it works** — The kayaker case study is offered as direct evidence for the general
biological principle that "the adaptive response induced by long-term training declines with
time" (Bouchard, 1986): diminishing returns set in within weeks, not months, for a fixed
training emphasis, which is the physiological argument for keeping each mesocycle-block short
and switching emphasis rather than running one long undifferentiated program.

**When to apply — Inference, mapped to a college football calendar** — **Fall camp** functions
as a short accumulation mesocycle at the low end of Issurin's range (closer to the 10-14 day
figure, or the 3-4 week figure if camp's aerobic/strength-base emphasis is counted from
voluntary summer conditioning): given the diminishing-returns pattern in the kayaker case
(most of a strength/aerobic gain arrives in the first 3-6 weeks), a multi-month, undifferentiated
summer conditioning block is exactly the pattern this framework argues against; a shorter,
concentrated base-building window, followed by a shift to more specific work, is the BPC
alternative. **The gap between the last regular-season/conference-championship game and a bowl
game** (commonly roughly 3-5 weeks for many programs) is long enough to support a short
accumulation mesocycle (10-14 to 20-25 days, matching both this section's end-of-season figure
and the mini-block interval used later in [[framework--prolonging-residual-effects-with-mini-blocks]])
if the goal is to rebuild any basic-ability deterioration accumulated over a long season before
shifting into a bowl-specific transmutation/realization sequence.

**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — The kayaker case study is a single unpublished thesis
(Sharobajko, 1984, a Ph.D. dissertation, Moscow All-Union Research Sport Institute), n = 8,
female kayakers, with no control group not receiving the same 20-week program; it demonstrates
a within-group improvement-rate curve, not a controlled comparison against an alternative
mesocycle length. **Population caveat:** this is Issurin's own book-wide pattern: the
accumulation-duration guidance and its supporting evidence are drawn from individual/endurance
Olympic sports (kayaking) tracking isometric strength and presumably aerobic markers, not from
any team-contact-sport population; football's basic-ability profile (short-duration high-force
efforts, position-specific demands, large roster with heterogeneous training age) is not
represented in this evidence base at all. The specific duration bands (six weeks / 3-4 weeks /
10-14 days) are Issurin's own applied judgment, not derived from a stated formula connecting
them to the kayaker data's exact decay curve.

**Example** — A 3-4 week early-summer strength-aerobic emphasis block, monitored against
Table 3.8's indicators (weekly key-lift totals, a repeated time-trial or aerobic test, resting
HR trend, body composition), gives a coach a citable structure for when to expect most of a
block's gain to already have happened (roughly the first half of the block, per the kayaker
curve) and when continuing the same emphasis is likely yielding only marginal further return.

14	# Transmutation Mesocycle: Capped at About Four Weeks by Fatigue and by the Aerobic Residual Clock
15	
16	**What it is** — The transmutation mesocycle "transmutes accumulated basic abilities into
17	specific physical and techno-tactical fitness" and is characterized by more specialized
18	targeted abilities, higher-intensity/higher-volume developmental workloads, and being "the most
19	fatiguing mesocycle" (PDF p. 118, printed p. 107; verified against page image). Table 3.9 gives
20	three duration-limiting factors: **fatigue accumulation** from highly concentrated intense
21	workloads approaches its upper limit in **3-4 weeks** (obviated by inserting a restorative
22	microcycle or an aerobic mini-block); **the residual training effect of the preceding
23	(accumulation) mesocycle**, since after 4 weeks of highly intense work the effect of the prior
24	aerobic-strength mesocycle "drops dramatically," per the roughly 30-day residual windows in
25	[[claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]]; and **the competition
26	calendar**, which can force a shorter mesocycle regardless of the other two factors. Net rule:
27	the transmutation mesocycle "usually lasts no more than four weeks" (PDF pp. 118-119, printed
28	pp. 107-108). Issurin flags a real methodical contradiction here: many sports need anaerobic
29	glycolytic development over a longer period than four weeks allows without letting the
30	accumulation mesocycle's aerobic/strength residual decay; the stated fix is inserting a
31	short aerobic mini-block inside the transmutation mesocycle (elaborated in
32	[[framework--prolonging-residual-effects-with-mini-blocks]]). Content (Table 3.10, PDF p. 119,
33	printed p. 108) sequences: an **initial** loading microcycle (usually one week) with gradually
34	increasing load; **mid-and-ending** loading and/or impact microcycles (impact can run 3-4 days);
35	and optional insertions, including a **competition/trial** microcycle (participating fatigued is
36	not excluded; athletes tend to experience the competitive workload itself as a relative load
37	reduction, and expect no personal best from it), a **restoration** microcycle (planned in
38	advance or triggered individually as athletes near their adaptation limit), or a short
39	**aerobic contrast mini-block** (2-4 days, to prolong aerobic training residuals and partly
40	restore athletes for the next high-intensity stretch). Monitoring (Table 3.11, PDF p. 120,
41	printed p. 109) again tracks workload performance, targeted (sport-specific) ability results,
42	and training responses, but with an added emphasis here: **subjective self-estimation of
43	fatigue, stress, sleep, and muscle soreness**, because "maximal workloads elicit maximal
44	training responses" and "much confidence between the coach and athlete is very important."
45	Because dosing near the "upper limits of adaptation" is described as the transmutation
46	mesocycle's biggest problem, Issurin gives Peter Snell's (Olympic champion runner and sport
47	physiologist) definition of overtraining: "a state in which performance diminishes while the
48	level of training is maintained or increased" (Snell, 1990), and lists five early warning
49	signals (Burke et al., 1990; Hooper et al., 1995, PDF p. 121, printed p. 110): resting HR up
50	more than **5 beats/min over 3-5 days**; persistent or rapid body-mass decrease; persistent
51	increased general fatigue; persistent increased muscle soreness; persistent increased sleep
52	disturbance. A supporting case study (Hooper et al., 1995, same locator): **19 elite swimmers**
53	monitored over 6 months with a large blood/urine/hormone/CPK/HR/blood-pressure battery plus
54	daily self-reported stress, fatigue, sleep quality, and muscle soreness (1-7 scale); **three**
55	swimmers were diagnosed overtrained during the study, but stale-vs-non-stale athletes did
56	**not** differ on any blood, urine, or physiological marker at mid- or late-season. The
57	difference showed up clearly and significantly only in the subjective fatigue/soreness
58	ratings, and a multi-component model using those four subjective ratings predicted competitive
59	performance changes; adding more objective indicators did not improve prediction accuracy.
60	
61	**Why it works** — The duration cap follows directly from stacking two decay clocks against
62	each other: fatigue from concentrated intense work saturates in 3-4 weeks, and the prior
63	mesocycle's basic-ability residual (aerobic endurance, max strength, ~30 days per
64	[[claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]]) also runs out around then, so
65	a transmutation mesocycle that runs longer risks both overtraining and arriving at competition
66	with degraded basic abilities. The Hooper et al. (1995) finding, that cheap subjective ratings
67	out-predicted an expensive blood/hormone panel, is presented as direct evidence that
68	systematic self-report monitoring is not a "budget substitute" for physiological testing in
69	this specific application; it is described as the more sensitive tool for catching overtraining
70	in this data set.
71	
72	**When to apply — Inference, mapped to a college football calendar** — The **middle-to-late
73	weeks of fall camp**, where two-a-days and the highest-intensity, most sport-specific
74	(scrimmage-heavy) work concentrate, are functionally a transmutation mesocycle and should be
75	capped near the same 3-4 week outer limit Issurin gives, both to avoid overtraining and because
76	any aerobic/strength base built in an early-camp or summer accumulation phase will itself decay
77	on roughly the same clock. Any old-school "keep hammering all camp" plan without at least one
78	built-in restorative window or aerobic mini-block runs against both duration-limiting factors
79	here at once. **Eric's baseline** does not name Snell's overtraining definition or the
80	five warning signs, but the department's stated preference for practical, athlete-reportable
81	signals over burdensome batteries (`method-baseline.md`, "Load monitoring and GPS," discussing
82	why daily wellness surveys were tried) is philosophically aligned with the Hooper et al.
83	finding, though see the "Contested" note below: the baseline corpus's own experience is that a
84	*specific* subjective wellness survey was later abandoned because athletes learned to game it.
85	
86	**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — **Population caveat:** every piece of supporting evidence
87	in this section (Sharobajko's kayakers referenced upstream, Hooper's 19 elite swimmers, Snell's
88	own middle-distance-running background) comes from individual endurance/technical sports, not
89	football; the 5 beats/min-over-3-5-days resting-HR threshold and the 3-4 week duration cap are
90	Issurin's own applied synthesis with no controlled dose-response citation. **Contested: this
91	frontmatter rating is set for the following specific conflict, not for the whole entry.** The
92	Hooper et al. (1995) result (subjective ratings beat objective blood/hormone markers for
93	overtraining detection) sits in direct tension with Eric's baseline's own SportSmith-documented
94	decision to replace subjective daily wellness surveys with objective force-plate mRSI,
95	specifically because "inconsistent data from a good test is still bad data" and subjective
96	self-report "couldn't be trusted" at scale (`method-baseline.md`, "Force plate and
97	neuromuscular monitoring" and "Philosophy and decision principles," citing
98	`2026-02-19-sportsmith-6otb-er.md` and `2026-02-20-sportsmith-6otb-nordbord-er.md`). This is
99	the same coach's-eye/subjective-vs-objective tension already logged in the baseline's own
100	"Tensions and contradictions" section (#3), now sharpened by a specific study on the Issurin
101	side of it. Do not treat either position as settled without discussing the difference in sample
102	size (n=19 vs. a 120+ player roster), duration (6 months vs. an academic year-plus), and survey
103	design (a validated multi-marker overtraining battery vs. a general daily wellness check); the
104	two findings could both be true of their own populations without either one generalizing to the
105	other.
106	
107	**Example** — A mid-fall-camp week showing a player's resting HR up 6 bpm over four days,
108	alongside self-reported fatigue and soreness climbing, would meet Issurin's stated early-warning
109	pattern for overtraining even before any blood marker moved. Per the Hooper et al. case,
110	that combination of signals, not a lab panel, is what caught it in the cited study.
111

13	
14	# Realization Mesocycle: One to Three Weeks, Much Lower Load, Built Around Maximal Speed and Rehearsed Competition Behavior
15	
16	**What it is** — The realization mesocycle is "traditionally... termed the taper" (PDF p. 122,
17	printed p. 111; verified against page image). In traditional periodization the taper only
18	precedes important competitions; under Block Periodization it is broader, forming the
19	concluding phase of **every** training stage (see
20	[[framework--training-stage-and-multi-peak-annual-cycle]]), so a season contains several
21	realization mesocycles of differing weight depending on the upcoming competition's importance.
22	Athletes enter this mesocycle fatigued from the preceding transmutation mesocycle, so the first
23	objective is restoration toward supercompensation by competition day; the targeted abilities
24	(maximal speed/quickness, event-specific tactics, competition readiness) all require high CNS
25	reactivity, available energy resources, and mental concentration, states only available to a
26	well-rested athlete, which is why workload reduction is described as "of paramount importance"
27	at the mesocycle's start. Table 3.12 (PDF p. 123, printed p. 112; verified against page image)
28	gives the full prescription: **aims**, peak-performance attainment, full restoration before
29	competition, and completing the training stage's overall program (peaking demands scale with
30	the competition's level/importance); **targeted abilities**, maximal speed/quickness,
31	event-specific tactics, readiness to compete; **workload level**, "much lower than in
32	preceding mesocycles," with various valid approaches to how that reduction is achieved;
33	**duration**, **one to three weeks**, depending on competition importance and sport-specific
34	factors; **techno-tactical improvement**, via sport-specific modeled exercises/tasks that must
35	build genuine competitive performance, not just rehearsal; **emotional tension/anxiety**,
36	elevates as competition approaches, more so for higher-stakes competition; **monitoring**,
37	follow-up time-trials, techno-tactical execution quality, training responses, and restoration
38	level, focused on integrative sport-specific estimates and each athlete's most important
39	individual traits; **nutrition**, deliberate use of supplements and energy-intake control to
40	produce an ergogenic effect and prevent unwanted body-composition change. On workload-reduction
41	timing: a **short** mesocycle demands a fast decrease; a **longer** one allows gradual
42	reduction; duration itself is "extremely important and sensitive" because a too-long taper
43	risks detraining while a too-short one may not restore and develop event-specific abilities
44	adequately (a contradiction Issurin attributes to Mujika et al., 2004). Techno-tactical
45	simulation must (1) reproduce the competitive situation as closely as possible, (2) approximate
46	competitive concentration levels, and (3) repeat enough to build stable, reliable skill. Table
47	3.13 (PDF p. 124, printed p. 113) gives a worked dosage for a **two-week realization mesocycle
48	for qualified kayakers**: quasi-competitive race performance, 4-6 total; race simulation in
49	broken series (four quarters, 20s breaks), 8-12; selective simulation of the initial race
50	quarter, 10-16; selective simulation of the two mid-race quarters, 8-12; simulation of the
51	pre-event warm-up program, 3-5. On emotional tension: pre-competition anxiety can cut either
52	way, moderate anxiety facilitates performance, excessive anxiety detracts from it, and elite
53	athletes are reported to benefit more from increased anxiety than sub-elite athletes, while
54	mid-class athletes can be "sharpened" by emotional tension (Raglin & Wilson, 2000, stated this
55	way in the source; the sub-elite/mid-class distinction is not further clarified there). Table
56	3.14 (PDF p. 125, printed p. 114) gives realization-specific monitoring indicators
57	(sprint-repetition and simulation totals; maximal-speed and event-simulation test results;
58	HR/blood lactate after relevant exercises; resting HR; sleep quality and mood questionnaire;
59	body mass and fat component). Issurin adds a specific nutrition warning, illustrated by a case
60	study: **20 highly qualified male long-distance triathletes**, tracked across a 4-week
61	high-workload mesocycle into a **2-week taper mesocycle** (PDF pp. 126-127, printed pp.
62	115-116, Figure 3.10, based on Margaritis et al., 2003): average energy intake stayed roughly
63	flat while energy expenditure fell by **up to 69.3%** during the taper; mean body mass didn't
64	change, but body fat mass **increased by 4.3%**. Issurin's point: unchanged body mass can mask
65	a real fat gain (or muscle loss) if eating habits don't adjust downward with the drop in
66	training energy cost, so body mass alone is "not always a reliable" anthropometric indicator
67	during a taper.
68	
69	**Why it works** — The core mechanism is the same reduced-load-toward-supercompensation logic
70	already given for the pre-competitive microcycle
71	(see [[framework--pre-competitive-microcycle-tuning]], which is this mesocycle's dominant
72	microcycle type): the targeted abilities need a well-rested nervous system and available energy
73	stores, so load must come down before those specific qualities can actually be trained and
74	expressed. The duration-sensitivity point (too long detrains, too short under-restores) is
75	Issurin's own applied synthesis, though he cites Mujika et al. (2004), a real, checkable
76	taper-physiology review, as the source flagging this contradiction in the field generally,
77	not something Issurin resolves with his own data here.
78	
79	**When to apply — Inference, mapped to a college football calendar** — **Bowl prep** is the
80	clearest college-football analog to a full one-to-three-week realization mesocycle: workload
81	should come down substantially from whatever preceded it (regular-season maintenance load, or a
82	short rebuild block if the last-game-to-bowl gap was used as a mini accumulation/transmutation
83	sequence, see [[framework--prolonging-residual-effects-with-mini-blocks]]), practice time
84	should shift toward maximal-speed/explosive work and heavily rehearsed, opponent-specific
85	game-plan simulation (the Table 3.13 dosage pattern, adapted from race-quarters to game-plan
86	segments, e.g., specific down-and-distance packages, specific special-teams looks), and staff
87	should watch emotional tension deliberately given a long layoff and a non-conference,
88	lower-frequency opponent-preparation rhythm. **The gap between the final regular-season/
89	conference-championship game and the bowl game** is exactly the scheduling problem Issurin's
90	duration-sensitivity warning describes: too long a "taper-only" approach across that whole gap
91	risks detraining (per Mujika et al., 2004, and consistent with
92	[[claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]]'s ~30-day residual windows for
93	basic abilities), which is the direct rationale for treating the early part of that gap as a
94	short accumulation/transmutation rebuild and only the final 1-3 weeks before the bowl as this
95	realization mesocycle. The nutrition warning (unchanged eating during a lower-workload window
96	risks fat gain even at stable body mass) is directly transferable to any football taper or bowl
97	prep window and worth flagging to Performance Nutrition specifically, since body-composition
98	oversight sits with that separate Health & Wellness unit per Eric's baseline
99	(`method-baseline.md`, "Nutrition and body composition"). **Eric's baseline** gives no duration
100	band or nutrition-adjustment guidance for a taper window anywhere in `method-baseline.md`; the
101	closest material is the general in-season rule "maintain intensity, reduce volume," citing
102	`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md` pp.20-21, which is compatible in direction but supplies
103	none of this entry's specificity (the one-to-three-week band, the competition-importance
104	scaling, or the body-composition-during-taper warning).
105	
106	**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — **Population caveat:** every piece of supporting data here
107	(the kayaker simulation dosage, the triathlete nutrition case) comes from individual endurance
108	sports with single, clearly-defined competitive efforts; football has no equivalent single
109	"race" to simulate, and a "game" cannot be rehearsed at full competitive intensity the way a
110	kayak race segment can. The triathlete case is n=20, one study, one sport, with no reported
