# Realization Mesocycle: One to Three Weeks, Much Lower Load, Built Around Maximal Speed and Rehearsed Competition Behavior

**What it is** — The realization mesocycle is "traditionally... termed the taper" (PDF p. 122,
printed p. 111; verified against page image). In traditional periodization the taper only
precedes important competitions; under Block Periodization it is broader, forming the
concluding phase of **every** training stage (see
[[framework--training-stage-and-multi-peak-annual-cycle]]), so a season contains several
realization mesocycles of differing weight depending on the upcoming competition's importance.
Athletes enter this mesocycle fatigued from the preceding transmutation mesocycle, so the first
objective is restoration toward supercompensation by competition day; the targeted abilities
(maximal speed/quickness, event-specific tactics, competition readiness) all require high CNS
reactivity, available energy resources, and mental concentration, states only available to a
well-rested athlete, which is why workload reduction is described as "of paramount importance"
at the mesocycle's start. Table 3.12 (PDF p. 123, printed p. 112; verified against page image)
gives the full prescription: **aims**, peak-performance attainment, full restoration before
competition, and completing the training stage's overall program (peaking demands scale with
the competition's level/importance); **targeted abilities**, maximal speed/quickness,
event-specific tactics, readiness to compete; **workload level**, "much lower than in
preceding mesocycles," with various valid approaches to how that reduction is achieved;
**duration**, **one to three weeks**, depending on competition importance and sport-specific
factors; **techno-tactical improvement**, via sport-specific modeled exercises/tasks that must
build genuine competitive performance, not just rehearsal; **emotional tension/anxiety**,
elevates as competition approaches, more so for higher-stakes competition; **monitoring**,
follow-up time-trials, techno-tactical execution quality, training responses, and restoration
level, focused on integrative sport-specific estimates and each athlete's most important
individual traits; **nutrition**, deliberate use of supplements and energy-intake control to
produce an ergogenic effect and prevent unwanted body-composition change. On workload-reduction
timing: a **short** mesocycle demands a fast decrease; a **longer** one allows gradual
reduction; duration itself is "extremely important and sensitive" because a too-long taper
risks detraining while a too-short one may not restore and develop event-specific abilities
adequately (a contradiction Issurin attributes to Mujika et al., 2004). Techno-tactical
simulation must (1) reproduce the competitive situation as closely as possible, (2) approximate
competitive concentration levels, and (3) repeat enough to build stable, reliable skill. Table
3.13 (PDF p. 124, printed p. 113) gives a worked dosage for a **two-week realization mesocycle
for qualified kayakers**: quasi-competitive race performance, 4-6 total; race simulation in
broken series (four quarters, 20s breaks), 8-12; selective simulation of the initial race
quarter, 10-16; selective simulation of the two mid-race quarters, 8-12; simulation of the
pre-event warm-up program, 3-5. On emotional tension: pre-competition anxiety can cut either
way, moderate anxiety facilitates performance, excessive anxiety detracts from it, and elite
athletes are reported to benefit more from increased anxiety than sub-elite athletes, while
mid-class athletes can be "sharpened" by emotional tension (Raglin & Wilson, 2000, stated this
way in the source; the sub-elite/mid-class distinction is not further clarified there). Table
3.14 (PDF p. 125, printed p. 114) gives realization-specific monitoring indicators
(sprint-repetition and simulation totals; maximal-speed and event-simulation test results;
HR/blood lactate after relevant exercises; resting HR; sleep quality and mood questionnaire;
body mass and fat component). Issurin adds a specific nutrition warning, illustrated by a case
study: **20 highly qualified male long-distance triathletes**, tracked across a 4-week
high-workload mesocycle into a **2-week taper mesocycle** (PDF pp. 126-127, printed pp.
115-116, Figure 3.10, based on Margaritis et al., 2003): average energy intake stayed roughly
flat while energy expenditure fell by **up to 69.3%** during the taper; mean body mass didn't
change, but body fat mass **increased by 4.3%**. Issurin's point: unchanged body mass can mask
a real fat gain (or muscle loss) if eating habits don't adjust downward with the drop in
training energy cost, so body mass alone is "not always a reliable" anthropometric indicator
during a taper.

**Why it works** — The core mechanism is the same reduced-load-toward-supercompensation logic
already given for the pre-competitive microcycle
(see [[framework--pre-competitive-microcycle-tuning]], which is this mesocycle's dominant
microcycle type): the targeted abilities need a well-rested nervous system and available energy
stores, so load must come down before those specific qualities can actually be trained and
expressed. The duration-sensitivity point (too long detrains, too short under-restores) is
Issurin's own applied synthesis, though he cites Mujika et al. (2004), a real, checkable
taper-physiology review, as the source flagging this contradiction in the field generally,
not something Issurin resolves with his own data here.

**When to apply — Inference, mapped to a college football calendar** — **Bowl prep** is the
clearest college-football analog to a full one-to-three-week realization mesocycle: workload
should come down substantially from whatever preceded it (regular-season maintenance load, or a
short rebuild block if the last-game-to-bowl gap was used as a mini accumulation/transmutation
sequence, see [[framework--prolonging-residual-effects-with-mini-blocks]]), practice time
should shift toward maximal-speed/explosive work and heavily rehearsed, opponent-specific
game-plan simulation (the Table 3.13 dosage pattern, adapted from race-quarters to game-plan
segments, e.g., specific down-and-distance packages, specific special-teams looks), and staff
should watch emotional tension deliberately given a long layoff and a non-conference,
lower-frequency opponent-preparation rhythm. **The gap between the final regular-season/
conference-championship game and the bowl game** is exactly the scheduling problem Issurin's
duration-sensitivity warning describes: too long a "taper-only" approach across that whole gap
risks detraining (per Mujika et al., 2004, and consistent with
[[claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]]'s ~30-day residual windows for
basic abilities), which is the direct rationale for treating the early part of that gap as a
short accumulation/transmutation rebuild and only the final 1-3 weeks before the bowl as this
realization mesocycle. The nutrition warning (unchanged eating during a lower-workload window
risks fat gain even at stable body mass) is directly transferable to any football taper or bowl
prep window and worth flagging to Performance Nutrition specifically, since body-composition
oversight sits with that separate Health & Wellness unit per Eric's baseline
(`method-baseline.md`, "Nutrition and body composition"). **Eric's baseline** gives no duration
band or nutrition-adjustment guidance for a taper window anywhere in `method-baseline.md`; the
closest material is the general in-season rule "maintain intensity, reduce volume," citing
`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md` pp.20-21, which is compatible in direction but supplies
none of this entry's specificity (the one-to-three-week band, the competition-importance
scaling, or the body-composition-during-taper warning).

**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — **Population caveat:** every piece of supporting data here
(the kayaker simulation dosage, the triathlete nutrition case) comes from individual endurance
sports with single, clearly-defined competitive efforts; football has no equivalent single
"race" to simulate, and a "game" cannot be rehearsed at full competitive intensity the way a
kayak race segment can. The triathlete case is n=20, one study, one sport, with no reported
statistical test of the 4.3% fat-mass change's significance in this text: treat the direction
(unadjusted eating during a taper risks fat gain) as a plausible, citable caution, not a
precise, guaranteed effect size for a football population with very different body-composition
targets and energy demands than a long-distance triathlete. The 1-3 week duration band and the
anxiety-by-athlete-level claim (Raglin & Wilson, 2000) are stated without further detail on
that study's own population or method in this text. This mesocycle's emotional-tension guidance
assumes a single identifiable peak competition; it does not address a multi-game bowl-adjacent
context (e.g., a conference championship immediately followed by a short turnaround into a
bowl selection process) where emotional tension may need to be managed across two closely
spaced high-stakes events rather than one clean taper.

**Example** — A three-week bowl-prep plan could open with a lighter first week (still
carrying some team-practice volume, closer to a short transmutation-mesocycle tail) that
tapers hard into a genuine one-to-two-week realization phase immediately before the game,
with practice time shifting toward explosive work and rehearsed, opponent-specific situational
football, energy intake reviewed alongside the drop in practice volume, and staff watching for
either excess complacency (too little anxiety, given the layoff and often lower-stakes framing
of some bowl games) or excess anxiety in players for whom the bowl carries personal stakes
(e.g., a senior's final game, an NFL draft evaluation window).

**Related** — [[framework--pre-competitive-microcycle-tuning]],
[[framework--prolonging-residual-effects-with-mini-blocks]],
[[framework--training-stage-and-multi-peak-annual-cycle]],
[[claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]],
[[supertraining--verkhoshansky/framework--fitness-fatigue-modeling-and-taper-timing]] (staging),
[[periodization--bompa/heuristic--fatigue-fitness-3to1-ratio]].

14	# Competing While Fatigued Erased Popov's Aerobic-Threshold Gains Within Days
15	
16	**What it is** — Issurin addresses whether competitions inside a training stage (not the
17	final target competition) help or hurt (PDF pp. 128-129, printed pp. 117-118). His position:
18	mid- and low-level competitions inside accumulation or transmutation mesocycles add useful
19	emotional diversity and elicit training responses that enrich adaptation, but highly intense
20	competitive efforts also trigger a stress-hormone response (catecholamines, cortisol) that
21	reinforces the catabolic process (Viru & Viru, 2001), can reduce muscle mass and maximal
22	strength, and, the specific mechanism named here, suppresses aerobic-enzyme activity and
23	mitochondrial oxidative capacity (Volkov, 1986), shortening the residual training effect of the
24	preceding mesocycle (citing Issurin & Lustig, 2004, the same paper behind
25	[[claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]]). The supporting case: Alexander
26	Popov's (Russia, multi-Olympic/World swimming champion) preparation was tracked with an
27	incremental stepwise swimming test measuring anaerobic threshold speed (blood lactate = 4 mM)
28	and the speed producing 8 mM lactate (the stated lower limit of highly intense glycolytic work).
29	Measurements were taken at the start of a highly concentrated aerobic mesocycle, again 10 days
30	later, and again a few days after Popov competed several times (Figure 3.11, PDF p. 129,
31	printed p. 118; verified against page image, adapted from Pyne & Touretski, 1993). Both
32	velocity markers rose substantially over the mesocycle's first 10 days, then **fell
33	substantially** after the competition. Issurin attributes this decline directly to the
34	competition-shortened residual, not to any change in training content.
35	
36	**Why it works — the author's own attributed mechanism, not independently re-derived here** —
37	Issurin's stated chain is: highly intense competitive effort triggers a stress-hormone response
38	that suppresses aerobic-enzyme and mitochondrial activity (citing Volkov, 1986), which is the
39	same physiological substrate underlying aerobic endurance's normal ~30-day residual
40	(see [[claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]]), so a hard competition
41	acts like an accelerant on that decay clock rather than a separate, independent event.
42	
43	**When to apply** — As a citable, named-athlete illustration for why a program including
44	in-season or in-training-stage competitive tests should expect some real cost to basic-ability
45	residuals, not treat competing as a free additional training stimulus. Directly supports the
46	caution already logged for the transmutation mesocycle
47	(see [[framework--transmutation-mesocycle-duration-and-overtraining-monitoring]]) about why
48	"including competition" is listed as an *option*, with tradeoffs, rather than an unqualified
49	recommendation. **Inference:** for football, this is a reason to expect that a physically
50	brutal, high-intensity early-season or mid-season game can measurably eat into whatever aerobic
51	or strength base was built in the preceding weeks, not just add acute fatigue that resolves in
52	a few days, which argues for the mini-block "topping up" logic in
53	[[framework--prolonging-residual-effects-with-mini-blocks]] being applied proactively after
54	unusually hard, high-intensity games, not only on a fixed calendar schedule.
55	
56	**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — This is a single elite swimmer's data, reported secondhand
57	(Pyne & Touretski, 1993, published via Issurin & Lustig, 2004), with no comparison athlete who
58	trained the same mesocycle without competing, and no statistical test of the pre/post-competition
59	change reported in this text: the chart (Figure 3.11) shows one athlete's trajectory, not a
60	group result. **Inference:** swimming's anaerobic-threshold/lactate-based test protocol has no
61	direct football analog; football has no simple single-modality repeated field test that isolates
62	"aerobic threshold" the way a stepwise swim test does, so this exact monitoring approach cannot
63	be copied, only the underlying caution (hard competition costs some residual) can be carried
64	over. This case does not address whether the effect is dose-dependent on competition intensity,
65	duration, or the athlete's fitness level entering the competition.
66	
67	**Example** — A strength staff noting that a physically demanding, high-effort game (e.g., a
68	triple-overtime contest, or a game following an unusually taxing travel/short-week schedule)
69	likely cost the team some of the conditioning base built the prior weeks has a named precedent
70	(Popov's threshold-speed decline) for treating that as a real, not just anecdotal, training-load
71	event worth a deliberate light aerobic "top-up" in the following week, rather than assuming a
72	normal recovery day fully addresses it.
73	
74	**Related** — [[claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]],
75	[[framework--transmutation-mesocycle-duration-and-overtraining-monitoring]],
76	[[framework--prolonging-residual-effects-with-mini-blocks]],
77	[[case-study--popov-aerobic-strength-microcycle]].

preceding mesocycle (citing Issurin & Lustig, 2004, the same paper behind
[[claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]]). The supporting case: Alexander

later, and again a few days after Popov competed several times (Figure 3.11, PDF p. 129,

that suppresses aerobic-enzyme and mitochondrial activity (citing Volkov, 1986), which is the
same physiological substrate underlying aerobic endurance's normal ~30-day residual
(see [[claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]]), so a hard competition

13	
14	# When a Training Stage Outruns the 30-Day Residual Clock, Insert a Mini-Block, Don't Just Add Workouts
15	
16	**What it is** — This section directly answers the mismatch already flagged in
17	[[framework--transmutation-mesocycle-duration-and-overtraining-monitoring]]: the accumulation
18	mesocycle's basic-ability residual runs out at about **30 days** (Table 1.6; see
19	[[claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]]), which caps how long the
20	following transmutation-plus-realization stretch can run before basic abilities decay below
21	target. But Issurin notes many sports need their transmutation mesocycle to run **3-4 weeks**
22	for anaerobic glycolytic development, and the realization mesocycle (taper) can run **about two
23	weeks**: together, roughly **five weeks**, which already exceeds the ~30-day strength-aerobic
24	residual (PDF pp. 129-130, printed pp. 118-119; verified against page image). Issurin's stated
25	fix: do **not** simply add extra aerobic or strength workouts into the transmutation mesocycle
26	to "top up" the decaying residual. This fails because the highly intense transmutation
27	mesocycle actively suppresses the immediate effect of aerobic training, and the anabolic
28	strength stimulus needs recovery time the transmutation mesocycle cannot spare. Instead, insert
29	a **special compact mini-block (a short microcycle)** dedicated to the decaying ability. Figure
30	3.12 (PDF p. 130, printed p. 119; verified against page image) diagrams the resulting pattern
31	for a training stage, in sequence: **accumulation** (high-volume basic aerobic-strength
32	workloads, **20-25 days**), then **transmutation** (highly intensive specific workloads,
33	**20-25 days**, with a **mini-block** insertion partway through), then **realization** (taper
34	and maximal speed, **10-16 days**), then **competition**. Issurin gives a worked contrast of two
35	real scheduling situations (PDF p. 131, printed p. 120): when two targeted competitions are only
36	**five to six weeks apart** (his cited example: kayaking's European and World Championships),
37	the fix is to compress the whole stage (10-14 days accumulation, 10-14 days transmutation, 8-10
38	days realization), short enough that the accumulation mesocycle's own residual still covers the
39	whole stage, so **no mini-block is needed at all**. When circumstances instead force a longer,
40	**7-9 week** training stage (his example: pre-Olympic preparation, where the international
41	calendar has no tune-up competitions before the Games), the recommended answer is to plan longer
42	mesocycles **and** include the mini-block, because a stage that long cannot otherwise carry the
43	accumulation-phase residual all the way to competition. The chapter's own summary restates the
44	placement rule concretely: an **aerobic mini-block can be inserted inside the transmutation
45	mesocycle**, and a **highly intense anaerobic mini-block can be inserted inside the realization
46	mesocycle** (PDF p. 132, printed p. 121): each mesocycle gets a short dose of whichever
47	ability it does not otherwise train, timed to arrive before that ability's own residual clock
48	runs out.
49	
50	**Why it works** — The reasoning is entirely about matching mini-block placement to what a
51	normal workout addition cannot achieve: a single or a few extra sessions of the decaying
52	modality, embedded inside a mesocycle whose entire design is optimized for a *different*
53	ability, gets swallowed by that mesocycle's dominant physiological demand (suppressed
54	aerobic adaptation under transmutation's glycolytic load; insufficient recovery for anabolic
55	strength work under either mesocycle's fatigue). A discrete mini-block, by contrast, is
56	short enough to insert without abandoning the surrounding mesocycle's main purpose, but is its
57	own coherent unit (its own brief loading-then-recovery structure) rather than scattered
58	single sessions, which is why Issurin insists on "not several additional workouts but a
59	special compact mini-block."
60	
61	**When to apply — this is the entry most directly responsive to the strength-and-conditioning
62	miss-log's "peaking phase structure for collegiate football" gap (logged 2026-09-03), and the
63	clearest football calendar mapping in this chapter — Inference throughout** —
64	
65	- **The gap between the final regular-season or conference-championship game and a bowl game**
66	  (commonly roughly 3-6 weeks depending on bowl selection and game date) is structurally the
67	  same scheduling decision Issurin poses in his worked example. A **short** gap (roughly
68	  5-6 weeks or less) should be handled like his compressed-stage case: run a short
69	  accumulation-transmutation-realization sequence sized to fit inside the gap (e.g., 10-14 days
70	  rebuild / 10-14 days sharpen / remaining days as realization/taper), in which case a
71	  strength-aerobic residual built at the very start plausibly survives to the bowl game without
72	  needing a mini-block. A **longer** gap (closer to 6+ weeks, which happens for some
73	  earlier-selected bowls) more closely resembles his 7-9 week pre-Olympic case: plan a longer
74	  rebuild phase **and** insert an aerobic (or strength) mini-block partway through the
75	  bowl-prep transmutation-equivalent work, specifically to protect the basic conditioning base
76	  built early in the gap from decaying below target by game day.
77	- **In-season, week to week:** [[case-study--popov-competition-shortens-residual-effects]]
78	  already shows that a hard game can itself accelerate residual decay; a bye week, or a week
79	  after an unusually taxing game, is a natural, calendar-given opportunity to run something like
80	  Issurin's aerobic mini-block (a few days of concentrated aerobic-strength work) to "top up" a
81	  basic-ability residual before it drops further, rather than treating every week's training
82	  content as identical regardless of how the prior weeks' games affected the athletes.
83	- **Eric's baseline** does not currently name a mini-block concept or an explicit bowl-prep
84	  periodization structure at all; this framework is the single most direct, numerically specific
85	  answer this ingest has produced to that gap, and should be flagged to Eric as a candidate
86	  structure to react to, not an already-adopted practice.
87	
88	**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — **Population caveat, repeated deliberately because this is
89	the chapter's central prescriptive claim:** every piece of evidence behind this framework
90	(the 30-day residual table, the kayaking/pre-Olympic worked examples, the Popov case) comes from
91	individual, endurance-or-technical Olympic sports with a fixed, known international competition
92	calendar set months or years in advance. Football's bowl-selection process is itself uncertain
93	until late in the season (a team does not always know its exact bowl date and opponent far in
94	advance), which makes pre-planning an exact-length rebuild-then-taper sequence harder than in

# When a Training Stage Outruns the 30-Day Residual Clock, Insert a Mini-Block, Don't Just Add Workouts

**What it is** — This section directly answers the mismatch already flagged in
[[framework--transmutation-mesocycle-duration-and-overtraining-monitoring]]: the accumulation
mesocycle's basic-ability residual runs out at about **30 days** (Table 1.6; see
[[claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]]), which caps how long the
following transmutation-plus-realization stretch can run before basic abilities decay below
target. But Issurin notes many sports need their transmutation mesocycle to run **3-4 weeks**
for anaerobic glycolytic development, and the realization mesocycle (taper) can run **about two
weeks**: together, roughly **five weeks**, which already exceeds the ~30-day strength-aerobic
residual (PDF pp. 129-130, printed pp. 118-119; verified against page image). Issurin's stated
fix: do **not** simply add extra aerobic or strength workouts into the transmutation mesocycle
to "top up" the decaying residual. This fails because the highly intense transmutation
mesocycle actively suppresses the immediate effect of aerobic training, and the anabolic
strength stimulus needs recovery time the transmutation mesocycle cannot spare. Instead, insert
a **special compact mini-block (a short microcycle)** dedicated to the decaying ability. Figure
3.12 (PDF p. 130, printed p. 119; verified against page image) diagrams the resulting pattern
for a training stage, in sequence: **accumulation** (high-volume basic aerobic-strength
workloads, **20-25 days**), then **transmutation** (highly intensive specific workloads,
**20-25 days**, with a **mini-block** insertion partway through), then **realization** (taper
and maximal speed, **10-16 days**), then **competition**. Issurin gives a worked contrast of two
real scheduling situations (PDF p. 131, printed p. 120): when two targeted competitions are only
**five to six weeks apart** (his cited example: kayaking's European and World Championships),
the fix is to compress the whole stage (10-14 days accumulation, 10-14 days transmutation, 8-10
days realization), short enough that the accumulation mesocycle's own residual still covers the
whole stage, so **no mini-block is needed at all**. When circumstances instead force a longer,
**7-9 week** training stage (his example: pre-Olympic preparation, where the international
calendar has no tune-up competitions before the Games), the recommended answer is to plan longer
mesocycles **and** include the mini-block, because a stage that long cannot otherwise carry the
accumulation-phase residual all the way to competition. The chapter's own summary restates the
placement rule concretely: an **aerobic mini-block can be inserted inside the transmutation
mesocycle**, and a **highly intense anaerobic mini-block can be inserted inside the realization
mesocycle** (PDF p. 132, printed p. 121): each mesocycle gets a short dose of whichever
ability it does not otherwise train, timed to arrive before that ability's own residual clock
runs out.

**Why it works** — The reasoning is entirely about matching mini-block placement to what a
normal workout addition cannot achieve: a single or a few extra sessions of the decaying
modality, embedded inside a mesocycle whose entire design is optimized for a *different*
ability, gets swallowed by that mesocycle's dominant physiological demand (suppressed
aerobic adaptation under transmutation's glycolytic load; insufficient recovery for anabolic
strength work under either mesocycle's fatigue). A discrete mini-block, by contrast, is
short enough to insert without abandoning the surrounding mesocycle's main purpose, but is its
own coherent unit (its own brief loading-then-recovery structure) rather than scattered
single sessions, which is why Issurin insists on "not several additional workouts but a
special compact mini-block."

**When to apply — this is the entry most directly responsive to the strength-and-conditioning
miss-log's "peaking phase structure for collegiate football" gap (logged 2026-09-03), and the
clearest football calendar mapping in this chapter — Inference throughout** —

- **The gap between the final regular-season or conference-championship game and a bowl game**
  (commonly roughly 3-6 weeks depending on bowl selection and game date) is structurally the
  same scheduling decision Issurin poses in his worked example. A **short** gap (roughly
  5-6 weeks or less) should be handled like his compressed-stage case: run a short
  accumulation-transmutation-realization sequence sized to fit inside the gap (e.g., 10-14 days
  rebuild / 10-14 days sharpen / remaining days as realization/taper), in which case a
  strength-aerobic residual built at the very start plausibly survives to the bowl game without
  needing a mini-block. A **longer** gap (closer to 6+ weeks, which happens for some
  earlier-selected bowls) more closely resembles his 7-9 week pre-Olympic case: plan a longer
  rebuild phase **and** insert an aerobic (or strength) mini-block partway through the
  bowl-prep transmutation-equivalent work, specifically to protect the basic conditioning base
  built early in the gap from decaying below target by game day.
- **In-season, week to week:** [[case-study--popov-competition-shortens-residual-effects]]
  already shows that a hard game can itself accelerate residual decay; a bye week, or a week
  after an unusually taxing game, is a natural, calendar-given opportunity to run something like
  Issurin's aerobic mini-block (a few days of concentrated aerobic-strength work) to "top up" a
  basic-ability residual before it drops further, rather than treating every week's training
  content as identical regardless of how the prior weeks' games affected the athletes.
- **Eric's baseline** does not currently name a mini-block concept or an explicit bowl-prep
  periodization structure at all; this framework is the single most direct, numerically specific
  answer this ingest has produced to that gap, and should be flagged to Eric as a candidate
  structure to react to, not an already-adopted practice.

**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — **Population caveat, repeated deliberately because this is
the chapter's central prescriptive claim:** every piece of evidence behind this framework
(the 30-day residual table, the kayaking/pre-Olympic worked examples, the Popov case) comes from
individual, endurance-or-technical Olympic sports with a fixed, known international competition
calendar set months or years in advance. Football's bowl-selection process is itself uncertain
until late in the season (a team does not always know its exact bowl date and opponent far in
advance), which makes pre-planning an exact-length rebuild-then-taper sequence harder than in
Issurin's kayaking example, where the championship dates are fixed well ahead of the season.
**Inference:** none of Issurin's specific day-counts (20-25 / 20-25 / 10-16 days; the 5-6 week
vs. 7-9 week contrast) were derived from or tested against a team-contact-sport calendar; they
should be treated as a structural template to adapt to football's specific bowl-selection
timeline and roster fatigue state at season's end (which is itself compounded by an already-long
season, unlike Issurin's examples where the "prior mesocycle" is a dedicated, undisturbed
accumulation block rather than 12+ weeks of in-season competition). The mini-block's own
duration is not specified numerically in this section (Issurin calls it a "short microcycle,"
consistent with the 2-4 day aerobic contrast mini-block already given in
[[framework--transmutation-mesocycle-duration-and-overtraining-monitoring]]'s Table 3.10):
treat 2-4 days as the applicable figure by cross-reference, not as independently stated here.

**Example** — For a 4-week gap between a team's last game and its bowl game, a plan following
this framework could run roughly 10-12 days rebuilding aerobic-strength base (accumulation),
10-12 days of sharpened, game-plan-specific and higher-intensity work (transmutation) with a
short 2-3 day aerobic mini-block inserted partway through that phase to protect the just-rebuilt
base, then a final 7-10 days as a realization/taper phase per
[[framework--realization-mesocycle-taper-prescription]], versus a 6-week gap, where the
accumulation and transmutation phases could each extend closer to Issurin's 20-25 day figures,
still with the mini-block insertion, since a stage that long cannot otherwise be covered by a
single unbroken residual window.

**Related** — [[claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]],

[[framework--training-stage-and-multi-peak-annual-cycle]].

# Issurin 2016 — Benefits and limitations of block-periodized preparation

> **Citation**
> Issurin, V. B. (2016). Benefits and limitations of block periodized training approaches to athletes' preparation: A review. *Sports Medicine, 46*(3), 329–338. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-015-0425-5

## Why it was promoted

This review distinguishes concentrated-unidirectional and multi-targeted block models and provides a useful conceptual vocabulary for discussing concentrated workloads and sequencing.

## Research question

What benefits, limitations, and sport-context boundaries are reported for two versions of block-periodized athlete preparation?

## Population and context

- The review emphasizes elite, subelite, and well-trained athletes across endurance, team, combat, dual, jumping, and strength/power settings. [p. 11]
- It also discusses a smaller number of recreational-athlete studies.
- It is a training-theory review, not evidence specific to collegiate American football.

## Study design and methods

- Narrative review contrasting concentrated-unidirectional and multi-targeted block-periodization models.
- The article summarizes prior studies in tables but does not report a systematic search, eligibility process, formal risk-of-bias appraisal, or meta-analysis.
- Consequently, the stated number and direction of supportive studies should be interpreted as an author-curated synthesis rather than a pooled comparative estimate.

## Key findings

- Concentrated-unidirectional programs in combat and team sports improved some fitness measures, but the reviewed studies did not report effects on team practice or competitive performance. [p. 6]
- In an elite-swimmer example, specific strength and anaerobic capacity improved but swimming performance improved in only two of three athletes. [p. 6]
- The author judged the concentrated-unidirectional evidence insufficient for broad implementation in high-performance combat, team-sport, and swimming preparation. [p. 6]
- The review reports support from 28 studies for multi-targeted block programs, but the designs, populations, outcomes, and comparator quality varied. [p. 11]
- The concentrated-unidirectional model was presented as better suited to sports dominated by a narrow target quality and as restricted when peak performance requires many interacting abilities. [p. 11]

## Limitations and applicability

- Non-systematic study selection and absent risk-of-bias assessment create a substantial risk of selective emphasis.
- Fitness improvements are not interchangeable with sport-specific performance, availability, or competitive outcomes. [p. 6]
- Training models were not consistently isolated from total volume, intensity, exercise choice, coaching, or athlete history.
- Evidence spans dissimilar sports and training levels; it does not supply validated block durations or effect estimates for collegiate American football.
- The strong conclusion favoring multi-targeted block periodization is the author's synthesis and should not be treated as settled comparative evidence. [p. 11]

## Practitioner interpretation

Use block periodization as a planning hypothesis: concentrate compatible emphases when competition structure and athlete needs justify it, while maintaining the qualities and technical exposure that cannot safely decay. Judge the plan by sport-specific performance, availability, and individual response—not by the periodization label. Compare it prospectively with the program's own prior practice where feasible.

## Evidence map

| Claim | Locator | Evidence type |
|---|---|---|
| Review scope and distinction between two models | p. 4 | narrative framing |
| Concentrated-unidirectional evidence and performance gaps | p. 6 | narrative synthesis |
| Multi-targeted evidence claim and applicability boundaries | p. 11 | narrative synthesis/limitation |

# "Adaptive Reconstruction" vs. "Supercompensation": Verkhoshansky/Siff's Sharper Critique

**What it is** — The authors argue "adaptive reconstruction" is a more accurate term than
"supercompensation" for the body's response to training load. One reason is stated
directly alongside the term: enhanced performance "is not simply the result of increased
stores of bioenergetic substances, but also of structural changes in muscle and other
tissues, as well as enhanced efficiency and rates of bioenergetic and neuromuscular
processing" (printed 84). A second reason comes not from that passage but from the
separate single-factor-model critique in 1.16.3: ATP "has never been shown to deplete
significantly, even after very strenuous exercise," and "no supercompensation has yet been
observed to occur among any of the other biochemicals" besides glycogen; each substance
returns to its initial level on its own timeline, so "the timing of subsequent loads to
stimulate the appropriate type of supercompensation remains indeterminate" (printed 87-88).

The book gives two different definitions of "Current Adaptation Reserves" (CAR) for
opposite ends of the same distinction: printed 83 states "In Russian texts, the former
[i.e. the readily-available, superficial] energy source is referred to as the Current
Adaptation Reserves (CAR)," while the Fig 1.39 caption on printed 84 states "The Deep
Adaptation Energy is often referred to as the Current Adaptation Reserves (CAR) by Russian
authors." Both are recorded here rather than harmonized.

The book also conflicts with itself on supercompensation: printed 85 (citing Platonov,
1988) states "supercompensation of some of the energy sources takes place," while printed
88 states "No supercompensation has yet been observed to occur among any of the other
biochemicals." (PDF pp. 94-99, printed pp. 83-88.)

**Why it works** — Inference: if supercompensation literally meant every adaptation-relevant
substance or structure overshoots baseline on a predictable clock, timing the next training
stimulus to "catch the peak" would be a precise science; the book's own admission that this
overshoot pattern is not established for biochemicals besides glycogen undercuts that
precision and supports treating "the next stimulus should land on a rebound" as a general
heuristic, not a substance-by-substance timing rule.

**When to apply** — This library already carries the supercompensation model in
[[periodization--bompa/principle--supercompensation-cycle]], which itself notes
"contemporary sport science largely prefers the fitness-fatigue (two-factor) model over
literal supercompensation" and recommends treating supercompensation "as a useful mental
model, not a measured prescription." **Inference:** this entry adds the specific mechanism
for that caution (structural/efficiency changes beyond energy stores, and the
glycogen-only overshoot finding) and the CAR terminology, which the Bompa entry does not
include; use both together rather than duplicating either.

**When NOT to apply** — This entry is rated `contested` because it is itself a critique of
a still widely-taught model (supercompensation), argued from a mix of established fact
(structural adaptation beyond energy stores) and an absence-of-evidence claim (no
overshoot observed for other biochemicals) that could be revised by newer measurement
techniques. **Inference:** don't treat "adaptive reconstruction" as a rejection of
periodization practice built on supercompensation timing; the text itself notes
supercompensation theory, despite its shortcomings, had a profound and still-useful impact
on periodization design.

**Example** — **Inference:** glycogen loading before an endurance event is a legitimate
application of true supercompensation; assuming a similarly precise "peak window" exists
for, say, connective tissue remodeling or neuromuscular efficiency gains is not supported
by the same evidence.

**Related** — [[periodization--bompa/principle--supercompensation-cycle]] (reciprocal link
recommended there: note that Supertraining Ch1.16 sharpens the "useful mental model, not a
measured prescription" caution with the specific glycogen-only-overshoot finding and the
CAR/adaptive-reconstruction terminology).

**What it is** — The Two-Factor (Fitness-Fatigue) Model treats preparedness at time t as
initial preparedness plus the summed effect of a slow-decaying fitness after-effect and a
faster-decaying fatigue after-effect, each with its own magnitude and decay-time constant
(Banister et al., 1992). Banister and Calvert (1980) originated this with the Training
Impulse (TRIMP), a quantified unit of training load used to model and predict elite
swimming performance from the fitness/fatigue balance. Zatsiorsky (1995) is cited for the
same 3:1 fitness-to-fatigue decay ratio already in this library's Bompa material. Later
research building on this model examined tapering specifically: Fitz-Clarke et al. (1991)
found presently accepted taper protocols may be too rigorous and short for best results,
and several studies (Zarkadas et al. 1995; Mujika et al. 1996; Shepley et al. 1992) found
that proper placement of training volume during a taper is a key optimization factor, with
high training volume in the days immediately preceding competition possibly detrimental to
performance. Different muscle groups recover heterochronically, which is why some Russian
restoration specialists deliberately avoid applying restorative methods (e.g. massage) to
every muscle group after every session, since supercompensation is reportedly more
pronounced with partial rather than total restoration. (PDF pp. 99-100, printed pp. 88-89.)

**Why it works** — Modeling preparedness as the sum of two exponentially-decaying
after-effects with different time constants gives periodization a quantitative structure

1	"""Extract a PDF into per-page text as JSON, and detect scanned/image PDFs.
2	Usage: python extract_pdf.py <book.pdf> [--pages A-B] [--probe]
3	Prefers pypdf; if absent, attempts pip install into user site at runtime.
4	--probe prints {"pages": N, "text_pages": K, "scanned": bool} and exits.
5	Page numbering (read this before citing pages):
6	- "page" is the 0-based PDF index (the first PDF page is 0). It stays 0-based so
7	  citations written by earlier ingests remain valid.
8	- "viewer_page" is page + 1: the number a PDF viewer and the Read tool show.
9	- --pages A-B takes 0-based indexes and is INCLUSIVE of both ends: --pages 12-20
10	  returns indexes 12 through 20 (9 pages). Before 2026-09-26 the end was exclusive,
11	  which silently dropped the last page of every range.
12	"""
13	import sys, json, subprocess
14	
15	def _ensure_pypdf():
16	    try:
17	        import pypdf  # noqa
18	        return
19	    except ImportError:
20	        subprocess.run([sys.executable, "-m", "pip", "install", "--quiet", "--user", "pypdf"], check=False)
21	
22	def load(path):
23	    _ensure_pypdf()
24	    from pypdf import PdfReader
25	    return PdfReader(path)
26	
27	def page_texts(reader):
28	    out = []
29	    for pg in reader.pages:
30	        try: out.append(pg.extract_text() or "")
31	        except Exception: out.append("")
32	    return out
33	
34	def main():
35	    args = sys.argv[1:]
36	    if not args:
37	        print("usage: extract_pdf.py <book.pdf> [--pages A-B] [--probe]", file=sys.stderr); sys.exit(2)
38	    path = args[0]
39	    reader = load(path)
40	    texts = page_texts(reader)
41	    if "--probe" in args:
42	        text_pages = sum(1 for t in texts if len(t.strip()) > 40)
43	        n = len(texts)
44	        scanned = n > 0 and (text_pages / n) < 0.2
45	        print(json.dumps({"pages": n, "text_pages": text_pages, "scanned": scanned}))
46	        return
47	    lo, hi = 0, len(texts)
48	    if "--pages" in args:
49	        rng = args[args.index("--pages") + 1]
50	        a, b = rng.split("-")
51	        lo, hi = int(a), int(b)
52	    # Inclusive end (fixed 2026-09-26; it was exclusive and dropped the last page).
53	    print(json.dumps([{"page": i, "viewer_page": i + 1, "text": texts[i]}
54	                      for i in range(max(lo, 0), min(hi + 1, len(texts)))], ensure_ascii=False))
55	
56	if __name__ == "__main__":
57	    main()

lines: **When to apply** — Any report or conversation where a device output is being used to say something about the athlete's internal state (fatigue, readiness, tissue tolerance) rather than just the output itself. **Eric's baseline:** modified reactive strength index (mRSI) from daily CMJ testing was deliberately chosen as the daily athlete-readiness marker in place of subjective wellness questionnaires, because it is "objective, consistent, and actionable in a way the wellness surveys never quite were" [method-baseline.md, Force plate and neuromuscular monitoring]. **Inference:** this framework's discipline would ask the same question of mRSI that Weber asks of his CMJ example, what is actually measured (jump-derived force/time output), and what is being inferred from it (neuromuscular readiness), stated with what confidence.

-**When NOT to apply** — This is a communication and reasoning discipline, not a claim that inference is unreliable or should be avoided; Weber's own examples (hamstring context: injury history, strength tests, jumping/hopping, speed exposure, running mechanics) show that combining several measurements to support one inference is the intended use, not a replacement for inference altogether (Lab 2A summary, 03:20–05:02). It also does not by itself tell you whether an observed change exceeds measurement noise — see [[framework--reliability-vs-sensitivity-mdc-and-swc]] for that separate question.

+**When NOT to apply** — This is a communication and reasoning discipline, not a claim that inference is unreliable or should be avoided; Weber's own examples (hamstring context: injury history, strength tests, jumping/hopping, speed exposure, running mechanics) show that combining several measurements to support one inference is the intended use, not a replacement for inference altogether (Lab 2A summary, 03:20–05:02). It also does not by itself tell you whether an observed change exceeds measurement noise: see [[framework--reliability-vs-sensitivity-mdc-and-swc]] for that separate question.

-# "Adaptive Reconstruction" vs. "Supercompensation": Verkhoshansky/Siff's Sharper Critique
-**What it is** — The authors argue "adaptive reconstruction" is a more accurate term than
-"supercompensation" for the body's response to training load. One reason is stated
-directly alongside the term: enhanced performance "is not simply the result of increased
-stores of bioenergetic substances, but also of structural changes in muscle and other
-tissues, as well as enhanced efficiency and rates of bioenergetic and neuromuscular
-processing" (printed 84). A second reason comes not from that passage but from the
-separate single-factor-model critique in 1.16.3: ATP "has never been shown to deplete
-significantly, even after very strenuous exercise," and "no supercompensation has yet been
-observed to occur among any of the other biochemicals" besides glycogen; each substance
-returns to its initial level on its own timeline, so "the timing of subsequent loads to
-stimulate the appropriate type of supercompensation remains indeterminate" (printed 87-88).
-The book gives two different definitions of "Current Adaptation Reserves" (CAR) for
-opposite ends of the same distinction: printed 83 states "In Russian texts, the former
-[i.e. the readily-available, superficial] energy source is referred to as the Current
-Adaptation Reserves (CAR)," while the Fig 1.39 caption on printed 84 states "The Deep
-Adaptation Energy is often referred to as the Current Adaptation Reserves (CAR) by Russian
-authors." Both are recorded here rather than harmonized.
-The book also conflicts with itself on supercompensation: printed 85 (citing Platonov,
-1988) states "supercompensation of some of the energy sources takes place," while printed
-88 states "No supercompensation has yet been observed to occur among any of the other
-biochemicals." (PDF pp. 94-99, printed pp. 83-88.)
-**Why it works** — Inference: if supercompensation literally meant every adaptation-relevant
-substance or structure overshoots baseline on a predictable clock, timing the next training
-stimulus to "catch the peak" would be a precise science; the book's own admission that this
-overshoot pattern is not established for biochemicals besides glycogen undercuts that
-precision and supports treating "the next stimulus should land on a rebound" as a general
-heuristic, not a substance-by-substance timing rule.
-**When to apply** — This library already carries the supercompensation model in
-[[periodization--bompa/principle--supercompensation-cycle]], which itself notes
-"contemporary sport science largely prefers the fitness-fatigue (two-factor) model over
-literal supercompensation" and recommends treating supercompensation "as a useful mental
-model, not a measured prescription." **Inference:** this entry adds the specific mechanism
-for that caution (structural/efficiency changes beyond energy stores, and the
-glycogen-only overshoot finding) and the CAR terminology, which the Bompa entry does not
-include; use both together rather than duplicating either.
-**When NOT to apply** — This entry is rated `contested` because it is itself a critique of
-a still widely-taught model (supercompensation), argued from a mix of established fact
-(structural adaptation beyond energy stores) and an absence-of-evidence claim (no
-overshoot observed for other biochemicals) that could be revised by newer measurement
-techniques. **Inference:** don't treat "adaptive reconstruction" as a rejection of
-periodization practice built on supercompensation timing; the text itself notes
-supercompensation theory, despite its shortcomings, had a profound and still-useful impact
-on periodization design.
-**Example** — **Inference:** glycogen loading before an endurance event is a legitimate
-application of true supercompensation; assuming a similarly precise "peak window" exists
-for, say, connective tissue remodeling or neuromuscular efficiency gains is not supported
-by the same evidence.
-**Related** — [[periodization--bompa/principle--supercompensation-cycle]] (reciprocal link
-recommended there: note that Supertraining Ch1.16 sharpens the "useful mental model, not a
-measured prescription" caution with the specific glycogen-only-overshoot finding and the
-CAR/adaptive-reconstruction terminology).

# Six Microcycle Types by Purpose and Load, With One-, Two-, and Three-Peak Weekly Load Waves

**What it is** — Table 3.1 (PDF p. 88, printed p. 77; verified against the page image)
gives six microcycle types, each with a stated purpose, load level, design particular, and
duration range: **Adjustment** (initial adaptation to loads, medium load, gradual workload
increase, **5-7 days**); **Loading** (fitness development, substantial-high load, big/substantial
workloads, **5-9 days**); **Impact** (fitness development via extreme stimuli, very
high-extreme load, summation of extreme workloads, **4-7 days**); **Pre-competitive**
(immediate preparation for competition, medium load, tuning with event-specific means,
**5-7 days**, see [[framework--pre-competitive-microcycle-tuning]] for full detail);
**Competitive** (participation in competition, high-very high load, sport/event-specific
performance, **2-7 days**); **Restoration** (active recovery, low load, wide spectrum of
restorative means, **3-7 days**). Issurin notes the adjustment microcycle can shorten to
3-5 days mid-season (e.g., starting a new training stage or a camp), and the restoration
microcycle after camp or competition typically runs 3-4 days mid-season (PDF p. 88, printed
p. 77). Separately, Issurin describes load variation **within** a microcycle as a "wave-shape
design" using the 5-point load scale from [[framework--workout-load-classification-and-rpe-mapping]]:
Figure 3.1 (PDF p. 90, printed p. 79) shows one-, two-, and three-peak weekly load patterns
for single-workout-per-day microcycles. Two- and three-peak designs are described as "used
most widely" because they let athletes handle a relatively large weekly workload with reduced
excessive-fatigue risk; the one-peak design concentrates several developmental workouts for a
"more profound and stressful training response," a pattern reserved for "sufficiently
prepared high-performance athletes" and not for novices. For microcycles with two workouts
per day, Figure 3.2 (PDF p. 91, printed p. 80) gives a worked ten-workout example: two
development workouts open the week (first peak), two medium-load supporting workouts
provide restoration, then a three-session mini-block including two key-workouts forms the
second peak, with the week's final session usable as a time-trial or scrimmage.

**Why it works** — Issurin frames the point-scale quantification (adapted from the 5-point
load scale) as serving three purposes: it lets coaches in non-measurable sports (sailing,
team/dual sports) express load numerically and visually; it lets athletes see and
consciously anticipate key-workouts and the restoration that follows load peaks
(a didactic use); and it lets whole microcycles be compared to each other for planning
purposes (PDF pp. 91-92, printed pp. 80-81). The peak/trough pattern itself follows the same
general logic as [[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]]: concentrating the
week's hardest sessions into one, two, or three peaks (rather than spreading maximal effort
evenly across every day) lets fatigue clear between peaks so each peak can still be
performed at a high standard.

**When to apply** — Classifying a week's purpose before assigning workouts to it (is this
week meant to adjust athletes to new load, develop fitness, deliver an extreme stimulus, tune
for competition, compete, or actively recover), and then shaping that week's daily load curve
around one, two, or three peaks depending on athlete level and the week's targeted abilities.
**Inference, mapped to a college football calendar:** early fall camp days function like
Issurin's **adjustment** microcycle (medium load, gradual ramp, until two-a-days are
tolerated); the heaviest camp week(s) resemble the **impact** type (very high-extreme load,
short duration, 4-7 days, matching the "impact week" concept sometimes used informally in
strength-staff planning); the week of the season opener and each bowl-prep week function as
**pre-competitive** microcycles (see [[framework--pre-competitive-microcycle-tuning]]); a
normal in-season game week is Issurin's **competitive** microcycle in form (the whole week
organized around one **competition**, 2-7 days), though its internal training content is
closer to what [[framework--in-season-team-sport-mini-block-microcycle]] describes; and a bye
week or the week after a game before a short turnaround functions as a **restoration**
microcycle. **Eric's baseline** does not currently name these six categories explicitly, but
the general planning language ("a 'training week' does not have to equal 7 calendar days,"

# Six Microcycle Types by Purpose and Load, With One-, Two-, and Three-Peak Weekly Load Waves

**What it is** — Table 3.1 (PDF p. 88, printed p. 77; verified against the page image)
gives six microcycle types, each with a stated purpose, load level, design particular, and
duration range: **Adjustment** (initial adaptation to loads, medium load, gradual workload
increase, **5-7 days**); **Loading** (fitness development, substantial-high load, big/substantial
workloads, **5-9 days**); **Impact** (fitness development via extreme stimuli, very
high-extreme load, summation of extreme workloads, **4-7 days**); **Pre-competitive**
(immediate preparation for competition, medium load, tuning with event-specific means,
**5-7 days**, see [[framework--pre-competitive-microcycle-tuning]] for full detail);
**Competitive** (participation in competition, high-very high load, sport/event-specific
performance, **2-7 days**); **Restoration** (active recovery, low load, wide spectrum of
restorative means, **3-7 days**). Issurin notes the adjustment microcycle can shorten to
3-5 days mid-season (e.g., starting a new training stage or a camp), and the restoration
microcycle after camp or competition typically runs 3-4 days mid-season (PDF p. 88, printed
p. 77). Separately, Issurin describes load variation **within** a microcycle as a "wave-shape
design" using the 5-point load scale from [[framework--workout-load-classification-and-rpe-mapping]]:
Figure 3.1 (PDF p. 90, printed p. 79) shows one-, two-, and three-peak weekly load patterns
for single-workout-per-day microcycles. Two- and three-peak designs are described as "used
most widely" because they let athletes handle a relatively large weekly workload with reduced
excessive-fatigue risk; the one-peak design concentrates several developmental workouts for a
"more profound and stressful training response," a pattern reserved for "sufficiently
prepared high-performance athletes" and not for novices. For microcycles with two workouts
per day, Figure 3.2 (PDF p. 91, printed p. 80) gives a worked ten-workout example: two
development workouts open the week (first peak), two medium-load supporting workouts
provide restoration, then a three-session mini-block including two key-workouts forms the
second peak, with the week's final session usable as a time-trial or scrimmage.

**Why it works** — Issurin frames the point-scale quantification (adapted from the 5-point
load scale) as serving three purposes: it lets coaches in non-measurable sports (sailing,
team/dual sports) express load numerically and visually; it lets athletes see and
consciously anticipate key-workouts and the restoration that follows load peaks
(a didactic use); and it lets whole microcycles be compared to each other for planning
purposes (PDF pp. 91-92, printed pp. 80-81). Issurin's own stated reason for the peak/trough
pattern itself: "The two or three load reductions facilitate athletes' restoration and
stimulate their readiness to effectively perform subsequent high demand workouts" (PDF p. 90,
printed p. 79). **Inference:** this is the same general logic as
[[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]] (concentrating the week's hardest sessions
into one, two, or three peaks, rather than spreading maximal effort evenly across every day,
lets fatigue clear between peaks so each peak can still be performed at a high standard), but
that link to the concentration principle is the writer's own connection, not a link Issurin
draws himself here.

**When to apply** — Classifying a week's purpose before assigning workouts to it (is this
week meant to adjust athletes to new load, develop fitness, deliver an extreme stimulus, tune
for competition, compete, or actively recover), and then shaping that week's daily load curve
around one, two, or three peaks depending on athlete level and the week's targeted abilities.
**Inference, mapped to a college football calendar:** early fall camp days function like
Issurin's **adjustment** microcycle (medium load, gradual ramp, until two-a-days are
tolerated); the heaviest camp week(s) resemble the **impact** type (very high-extreme load,
short duration, 4-7 days, matching the "impact week" concept sometimes used informally in
strength-staff planning); the week of the season opener and each bowl-prep week function as
**pre-competitive** microcycles (see [[framework--pre-competitive-microcycle-tuning]]); a
normal in-season game week is Issurin's **competitive** microcycle in form (the whole week
organized around one **competition**, 2-7 days), though its internal training content is
closer to what [[framework--in-season-team-sport-mini-block-microcycle]] describes; and a bye
week or the week after a game before a short turnaround functions as a **restoration**
microcycle. **Eric's baseline** does not currently name these six categories explicitly, but
the general planning language ("a 'training week' does not have to equal 7 calendar days,"
`method-baseline.md`, "Periodization and programming," citing week1-lecture.md p.39) is
consistent with treating microcycle type, not just calendar week, as the planning unit.

**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — The six-type table's specific duration ranges are
Issurin's own applied categorization; no citation or derivation is given for why, e.g., the
loading type is 5-9 days rather than some other range. **Inference:** none of the six types
or the one-/two-/three-peak wave figures are demonstrated on a team-sport example in this

sport contexts, and the specific number-of-peaks guidance ("one-peak... not [for] novice and
less prepared athletes") is stated for individual-sport training loads, not validated for a
100+ player roster with heterogeneous training ages. The point-scale system inherits every
limitation already logged for the underlying RPE/restoration-time scale in
[[framework--workout-load-classification-and-rpe-mapping]] (subjective, no cited validation
of the specific cut-points).

microcycle in the week before the opener, each transition marked by a deliberate change in
purpose and load level, not just a generic "camp is getting harder" narrative.

# Six Microcycle Types by Purpose and Load, With One-, Two-, and Three-Peak Weekly Load Waves

**What it is** — Table 3.1 (PDF p. 88, printed p. 77; verified against the page image)
gives six microcycle types, each with a stated purpose, load level, design particular, and
duration range: **Adjustment** (initial adaptation to loads, medium load, gradual workload
increase, **5-7 days**); **Loading** (fitness development, substantial-high load, big/substantial
workloads, **5-9 days**); **Impact** (fitness development via extreme stimuli, very
high-extreme load, summation of extreme workloads, **4-7 days**); **Pre-competitive**
(immediate preparation for competition, medium load, tuning with event-specific means,
**5-7 days**, see [[framework--pre-competitive-microcycle-tuning]] for full detail);
**Competitive** (participation in competition, high-very high load, sport/event-specific
performance, **2-7 days**); **Restoration** (active recovery, low load, wide spectrum of
restorative means, **3-7 days**). Issurin notes the adjustment microcycle can shorten to
3-5 days mid-season (e.g., starting a new training stage or a camp), and the restoration
microcycle after camp or competition typically runs 3-4 days mid-season (PDF p. 88, printed
p. 77). The impact microcycle specifically needs a special restoration program (diet,
supplements, hydrotherapy, massage, mental relaxation) "in order to fulfill their goals"
(PDF p. 89, printed p. 78). Separately, Issurin describes load variation **within** a microcycle as a "wave-shape
design" using the 5-point load scale from [[framework--workout-load-classification-and-rpe-mapping]]:
Figure 3.1 (PDF p. 90, printed p. 79) shows one-, two-, and three-peak weekly load patterns
for single-workout-per-day microcycles. Two- and three-peak designs are described as "used
most widely" because they let athletes handle a relatively large weekly workload with reduced
excessive-fatigue risk; the one-peak design concentrates several developmental workouts for a
"more profound and stressful training response," a pattern reserved for "sufficiently
prepared high-performance athletes" and not for novices. For microcycles with two workouts
per day, Figure 3.2 (PDF p. 91, printed p. 80) gives a worked ten-workout example: two
development workouts open the week (first peak), two medium-load supporting workouts
provide restoration, then a three-session mini-block including two key-workouts forms the
second peak, with the week's final session usable as a time-trial or scrimmage.

**Why it works** — Issurin frames the point-scale quantification (adapted from the 5-point
load scale) as serving three purposes: it lets coaches in non-measurable sports (sailing,
team/dual sports) express load numerically and visually; it lets athletes see and
consciously anticipate key-workouts and the restoration that follows load peaks
(a didactic use); and it lets whole microcycles be compared to each other for planning
purposes (PDF pp. 91-92, printed pp. 80-81). Issurin's own stated reason for the peak/trough
pattern itself: "The two or three load reductions facilitate athletes' restoration and
stimulate their readiness to effectively perform subsequent high demand workouts" (PDF p. 90,
printed p. 79). **Inference:** this is the same general logic as
[[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]] (concentrating the week's hardest sessions
into one, two, or three peaks, rather than spreading maximal effort evenly across every day,
lets fatigue clear between peaks so each peak can still be performed at a high standard), but
that link to the concentration principle is the writer's own connection, not a link Issurin
draws himself here.

**When to apply** — Classifying a week's purpose before assigning workouts to it (is this
week meant to adjust athletes to new load, develop fitness, deliver an extreme stimulus, tune
for competition, compete, or actively recover), and then shaping that week's daily load curve
around one, two, or three peaks depending on athlete level and the week's targeted abilities.
**Inference, mapped to a college football calendar:** early fall camp days function like
Issurin's **adjustment** microcycle (medium load, gradual ramp, until two-a-days are
tolerated); the heaviest camp week(s) resemble the **impact** type (very high-extreme load,
short duration, 4-7 days); the week of the season opener and each bowl-prep week function as
**pre-competitive** microcycles (see [[framework--pre-competitive-microcycle-tuning]]); a
normal in-season game week is closest to Issurin's separate 3.1.7 maintenance design for
team and dual sports, not Table 3.1's **competitive** type (which Issurin defines narrowly as
"participation in competition," with high to very high load, PDF p. 88, printed p. 77) — see
[[framework--in-season-team-sport-mini-block-microcycle]] for that design; and a bye week or
the week after a game before a short turnaround functions as a **restoration** microcycle. **Eric's baseline** does not currently name these six categories explicitly, but
the general planning language ("a 'training week' does not have to equal 7 calendar days,"
`method-baseline.md`, "Periodization and programming," citing week1-lecture.md p.39) is
consistent with treating microcycle type, not just calendar week, as the planning unit.

**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — The six-type table's specific duration ranges are
Issurin's own applied categorization; no citation or derivation is given for why, e.g., the
loading type is 5-9 days rather than some other range. **Inference:** none of the six types
or the one-/two-/three-peak wave figures are demonstrated on a team-sport example in this
section (that comes later, 3.1.7); the load-wave figures here are drawn from individual/dual
sport contexts, and the specific number-of-peaks guidance ("one-peak... not [for] novice and
less prepared athletes") is stated for individual-sport training loads, not validated for a
100+ player roster with heterogeneous training ages. The point-scale system inherits every
limitation already logged for the underlying RPE/restoration-time scale in
[[framework--workout-load-classification-and-rpe-mapping]] (subjective, no cited validation
of the specific cut-points).

**Example** — A four-week fall-camp block could be read as adjustment (days 1-5, single
practices, medium load) into loading (days 6-14, one-a-days plus early two-a-days) into an
impact microcycle (the hardest stretch of two-a-days, 4-7 days) into a pre-competitive
microcycle in the week before the opener, each transition marked by a deliberate change in
purpose and load level, not just a generic "camp is getting harder" narrative.

**Related** — [[framework--workout-load-classification-and-rpe-mapping]] (the 5-point scale
this section's point-quantification is built on), [[framework--pre-competitive-microcycle-tuning]],
[[framework--in-season-team-sport-mini-block-microcycle]],
[[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]],
[[framework--key-workout-and-key-exercise-concept]].

**What it is** — Issurin presents Alexander Popov's (Russia, multi-Olympic/World 50-100m
Freestyle swimming champion) typical strength-aerobic microcycle from his preparatory phase
(the accumulation mesocycle, in Block Periodization terms) as an example (PDF pp. 92-94,
printed pp. 81-83, Figure 3.3 and Table 3.2; sourced to "courtesy of Gennadi Touretski,
personal communication," Popov's coach). Across ten workouts, anaerobic threshold (AT) work
and technical stroke-count drills dominated; maximal-speed (alactic) exercises appeared daily
in medium proportions; aerobic power (AP) work appeared in only three workouts; strength
endurance (speed-resisted) drills were a large contributor; and anaerobic glycolytic (AnG)
work appeared **once**, in a 200m stepwise all-out time trial. Issurin's three stated
takeaways: (a) even for a prominent sprinter, aerobic-endurance volume is very high in this
microcycle; (b) strength can be developed effectively through force accentuation inside
sport-specific drills rather than only in the weight room; (c) despite 100m Freestyle's high
metabolic reliance on anaerobic glycolytic power/capacity, glycolytic *training* volume in
this aerobic microcycle is negligible, reserved instead for the anaerobic microcycle (see
[[framework--anaerobic-glycolytic-microcycle-design]]).

that concurrent aerobic stimulus improves oxidative support in the muscle mass strength

increases in comparison to strength training alone" (Zatsiorsky, 1985, PDF p. 92, printed
p. 81).

testosterone/cortisol citation: an anabolic hormonal environment is a precondition for the
strength stimulus to "take," and that environment is temporarily suppressed right after
exhaustive endurance work.

# Popov's Aerobic Microcycle: Anaerobic Glycolytic Work Is Nearly Absent Even for a 100m Freestyle Sprinter

**What it is** — Issurin presents Alexander Popov's (Russia, multi-Olympic/World 50-100m
Freestyle swimming champion) typical strength-aerobic microcycle from his preparatory phase
(the accumulation mesocycle, in Block Periodization terms) as an example (PDF pp. 92-94,
printed pp. 81-83, Figure 3.3 and Table 3.2; sourced to "courtesy of Gennadi Touretski,
personal communication," Popov's coach). Across ten workouts, anaerobic threshold (AT) work
and technical stroke-count drills dominated; maximal-speed (alactic) exercises appeared daily
in medium proportions; aerobic power (AP) work appeared in only three workouts; strength
endurance (speed-resisted) drills were a large contributor; and anaerobic glycolytic (AnG)
work appeared **once**, in a 200m stepwise all-out time trial. Issurin's three stated
takeaways: (a) even for a prominent sprinter, aerobic-endurance volume is very high in this
microcycle; (b) strength can be developed effectively through force accentuation inside
sport-specific drills rather than only in the weight room; (c) despite 100m Freestyle's high
metabolic reliance on anaerobic glycolytic power/capacity, glycolytic *training* volume in
this aerobic microcycle is negligible, reserved instead for the anaerobic microcycle (see
[[framework--anaerobic-glycolytic-microcycle-design]]). Table 3.2 (PDF p. 95, printed p. 84)
lists the compatible secondary modalities for an aerobic microcycle: maximum strength (first
priority; combining aerobic and strength work "ensures better oxidation in enlarged
muscles"), anaerobic alactic/maximum speed (sprints "break monotony and activate a wide
spectrum of muscle fibers... exploited in subsequent aerobic workloads"), aerobic
strength-endurance (speed-resisted exercises), and movement technique (drilled during
prolonged aerobic work without aggravating metabolic adaptation). Issurin adds a specific
timing rule: strength work should not follow directly after exhaustive aerobic training,
because the testosterone/cortisol ratio needed for protein synthesis stays depressed for
"many hours" post-endurance-work (Viru, Karelson & Smirnova, 1992); **24 hours** of recovery,
with only low-level loads in between, is stated as the needed gap (PDF p. 95, printed p. 84,
citing Chesley et al., 1992 for protein-turnover persisting ≥24 hours post-resistance-work).

**Why it works** — Issurin's own stated mechanism for combining aerobic and strength work is
that concurrent aerobic stimulus improves oxidative support in the muscle mass strength
training builds, addressing the problem (raised in Chapter 1's swimmer interference case,
[[case-study--concurrent-training-interference-and-decay]]) that strength-built muscle mass
without matched aerobic enzyme/mitochondrial development doesn't help endurance-sport
performance. The 24-hour strength-after-aerobic sequencing rule follows directly from the
testosterone/cortisol citation: an anabolic hormonal environment is a precondition for the
strength stimulus to "take," and that environment is temporarily suppressed right after
exhaustive endurance work.

**When to apply** — Designing an aerobic-base microcycle (early accumulation mesocycle, see
[[framework--accumulation-mesocycle-duration-and-monitoring]]) for any athlete needing both an
aerobic base and strength, and specifically the 24-hour strength-after-aerobic spacing rule
whenever a hard conditioning session and a strength session are close together in the same
microcycle. **Inference:** for football specifically, this example argues against treating
"conditioning day" and "lift day" as interchangeable slots without checking the sequencing
gap, particularly early in an off-season aerobic-base block.

**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — This is a single elite swimmer's program, reported
secondhand by his personal coach with no comparison data and no other athletes' programs
shown; it is Issurin's chosen illustrative anecdote, not a study. **Inference:** swimming's
metabolic and technical demands (continuous, cyclical, non-contact, highly technique-limited)
differ substantially from football; the specific finding that glycolytic training is nearly
absent in this microcycle should not be read as "football conditioning should minimize
glycolytic work"; Eric's baseline's own stated fall-camp priority stack treats glycolytic
conditioning as something to "absorb incidentally through camp and practice" rather than
program directly (`method-baseline.md`, "Conditioning and energy systems," citing
`class-4-2026.md` pp.34, 39), which is a different reason (practical prioritization under a
tight camp calendar) than Popov's reason (protecting a compatible-modality structure within
one microcycle type). The 24-hour strength-after-aerobic figure rests on two cited studies
(Viru et al. 1992; Chesley et al. 1992) not detailed further in this text: treat the
direction as supported but the exact "24 hours" as an applied rule of thumb, not a
precisely-dosed threshold verified here.

**Example** — A Baylor off-season aerobic-base week could sequence a hard aerobic-threshold
run or bike session on Monday, hold Tuesday's strength session to low-intensity technique
work only, and place the next true max-strength session on Wednesday (at least 24 hours after
Monday's endurance work, per the cited protein-turnover window), rather than programming a
hard conditioning session the evening before a heavy squat day.

**Related** — [[framework--anaerobic-glycolytic-microcycle-design]],
[[case-study--concurrent-training-interference-and-decay]],
[[framework--accumulation-mesocycle-duration-and-monitoring]],
[[principle--training-modality-compatibility-in-a-workout]].
