# Popov's Aerobic Microcycle: Anaerobic Glycolytic Work Is Nearly Absent Even for a 100m Freestyle Sprinter

**What it is** — Issurin presents Alexander Popov's (Russia, multi-Olympic/World 50-100m
Freestyle swimming champion) typical strength-aerobic microcycle from his preparatory phase
(the accumulation mesocycle, in Block Periodization terms) as an example (PDF pp. 92-94,
printed pp. 81-83, Figure 3.3 and Table 3.2; sourced to "courtesy of Gennadi Touretski,
personal communication" — the book does not itself state that Touretski was Popov's coach,
though that is a matter of public record). Across ten workouts, anaerobic threshold (AT) work
and technical stroke-count drills dominated; maximal-speed (alactic) exercises appeared daily
in medium proportions; aerobic power (AP) work appeared in only three workouts; strength
endurance (speed-resisted) drills were a large contributor; and anaerobic glycolytic (AnG)
work appeared **once**, in a 200m stepwise all-out time trial. Issurin's three stated
takeaways: (a) even for a prominent sprinter, aerobic-endurance volume is very high in this
microcycle; (b) strength abilities can be effectively developed by means of force accentuation
in sport-specific drills; (c) despite 100m Freestyle's high metabolic reliance on anaerobic
glycolytic power/capacity, glycolytic *training* volume in this aerobic microcycle is
negligible, reserved instead for the anaerobic microcycle (see
[[framework--anaerobic-glycolytic-microcycle-design]]). Table 3.2 (PDF p. 95, printed p. 84)
lists the compatible secondary modalities for an aerobic microcycle: maximum strength (first
priority; combining aerobic and strength work "ensures better oxidation in enlarged
muscles"), anaerobic alactic/maximum speed (sprints "break monotony and activate a wide
spectrum of muscle fibers... exploited in subsequent aerobic workloads"), aerobic
strength-endurance (speed-resisted exercises), and movement technique (drilled during
prolonged aerobic work without aggravating metabolic adaptation). Issurin adds a specific
timing rule: developing max-strength work should not follow directly after exhaustive
aerobic training, because the testosterone/cortisol ratio needed for protein synthesis stays
depressed for "many hours" post-endurance-work (Viru, Karelson & Smirnova, 1992); **24 hours**
of recovery, with only low-level loads in between, is stated as the needed gap (PDF p. 95,
printed p. 84, citing Chesley et al., 1992 for protein-turnover persisting ≥24 hours
post-resistance-work). This rule is scoped to developing max-strength sessions specifically:
Figure 3.4 (PDF p. 96, printed p. 85) still places medium- or substantial-load MS sessions in
the afternoon of the same day as a morning AE session (Mon, Thu), and the week's key MS
workout (Wed AM) sits roughly 24 hours after the key AE workout (Tue AM), with only a
low-load session between them.

**Why it works** — Issurin's own stated mechanism for combining aerobic and strength work is
that concurrent aerobic stimulus improves oxidative support in the muscle mass strength
training builds. **Inference:** this addresses a related but not identical problem raised in
Chapter 1's swimmer interference case
([[case-study--concurrent-training-interference-and-decay]]): that case is aerobic work
suppressing a strength adaptation, while this microcycle's problem (PDF pp. 92-94, printed
pp. 81-83) runs the other direction, enlarged muscle mass lacking the matched oxidative
capacity to be useful for endurance performance.
Issurin's own stated reason for excluding glycolytic work: "the athlete's body can not
respond effectively to training stimuli that simultaneously affect very different
physiological systems. Highly intense glycolitic workloads cause a profound metabolic
response and hormonal shift that can last two-three days (Viru, 1995) ... The addition of
anaerobic glycolitic workloads, however, leads to a disruption in metabolic adaptation and
dramatically decreases the cumulative training effect" (PDF pp. 93-94, printed pp. 82-83).
The combination also carries a stated cost: aerobic-strength work "reduces strength
increases in comparison to strength training alone" (Zatsiorsky, 1985, PDF p. 92, printed
p. 81).
The 24-hour strength-after-aerobic sequencing rule follows directly from the
testosterone/cortisol citation: an anabolic hormonal environment is a precondition for the
strength stimulus to "take," and that environment is temporarily suppressed right after
exhaustive endurance work.

**When to apply** — Designing an aerobic-base microcycle (early accumulation mesocycle, see
[[framework--accumulation-mesocycle-duration-and-monitoring]]) for any athlete needing both an
aerobic base and strength, and specifically the 24-hour developing-max-strength-after-aerobic
spacing rule whenever a hard conditioning session and a developing max-strength session are
close together in the same microcycle (Figure 3.4 shows the rule applies to the week's key
max-strength workout, not to every strength-modality session that day). **Inference:** for
football specifically, this example argues against treating "conditioning day" and "lift day"
as interchangeable slots without checking the sequencing gap, particularly early in an
off-season aerobic-base block.

**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — This is a single elite swimmer's program, reported
secondhand by his personal coach with no comparison data and no other athletes' programs

precisely-dosed threshold verified here.

work only, and place the next true max-strength session on Wednesday (at least 24 hours after

hard conditioning session the evening before a heavy squat day.

# The Anaerobic Glycolytic Microcycle Trades Restoration for Fatigue-Tolerant, Lactate-Driven Development

**What it is** — Issurin describes the microcycle that forms the content of the transmutation
mesocycle (PDF pp. 97-100, printed pp. 86-89, Table 3.3 and Figure 3.5). Its compatible
modalities (Table 3.3): **strength endurance** (mostly anaerobic; high-resistance drills
inside regular workouts or separate sessions; produces a dual strength-endurance and
anaerobic-metabolism effect), **anaerobic alactic/maximal speed** (used by moderately fatigued
athletes since a well-restored state is usually unavailable here; sprints add diversity and
short-duration power contribution), **low-intensity aerobic exercise** (used throughout as
active restoration, alongside stretching/relaxation), **movement technique** (fatigue
"suppress[es] technical skills; specific measures are necessary" to protect it, Table 3.3),
and **tactics** (given prime placement "both in the session and microcycle," treated as
essential despite metabolic fatigue because competition itself imposes comparable fatigue on
tactical execution). Issurin gives specific lactate-based intensity
zones: workloads producing **5-8 mM** blood lactate improve maximal aerobic power and
aerobic-anaerobic interaction and are more typical early-to-mid-season; workloads above
**8 mM** target anaerobic glycolytic power/capacity specifically and "contribute greatly" in
the final weeks before the target competition (PDF pp. 97-98, printed pp. 86-87). The worked ten-workout
chart (Figure 3.5, PDF p. 100, printed p. 89) uses a three-peak load design with six
development workouts (three of them key-workouts) targeting anaerobic glycolytic power,
anaerobic glycolytic capacity, and strength endurance, buffered by a mid-week restoration
"window" (Wednesday evening) and two medium-load alactic-maintenance sessions.

**Why it works** — Issurin states the defining feature of this microcycle is fatigue
accumulation with insufficient restoration by design (PDF p. 99, printed p. 88): high-load
glycolytic work drives maximal heart rate/cardiac output, maximal oxygen deficit/debt and
blood lactate accumulation, plus a rise in catecholamines and cortisol with testosterone
suppressed for 24+ hours (citing Viru, 1995). At a workout frequency of 6-12 sessions/week,
fatigue accumulation across the microcycle is "inevitable": the design goal is to manage that
fatigue (through workout sequencing, deliberately-placed restoration, and monitoring) rather
than to avoid it, which is what distinguishes this microcycle from the aerobic one.

**When to apply** — Structuring the highest-intensity block of a transmutation mesocycle
(see [[framework--transmutation-mesocycle-duration-and-overtraining-monitoring]]) when the
targeted abilities are anaerobic glycolytic power/capacity and anaerobic-component strength
endurance. Issurin's four stated guidelines for managing the built-in fatigue (PDF p. 99,
printed p. 88): sequence development workouts with expected fatigue accumulation in mind;
treat restoration workouts as a planned, non-optional part of the week; use active
restoration means (stretching, low-intensity drills, massage, physiotherapy, nutritional
support); and prioritize training-response monitoring here specifically. **Inference:** this
maps to the hardest week(s) of fall camp or a mid-season "gut check" conditioning emphasis,
where the department accepts several days of accumulating fatigue in exchange for a
concentrated glycolytic-capacity stimulus, rather than trying to keep every day fresh.

**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — The specific lactate cut-points (5-8 mM vs. >8 mM) and
the 6-12 workouts/week frequency figure are presented without a cited validation study in this
passage; treat them as Issurin's own applied heuristics. **Inference:** the book names team
sports twice in this section — the tactics row is "focus[ed] on dual and team sports and
combat sports" (Table 3.3, PDF p. 97, printed p. 86), and "the specific demands of several
sports (in particular team and dual sports and combat sports) dictate involvement of
short-duration bouts (alactic) and more prolonged efforts (glycolitic)" (PDF p. 98, printed
p. 87) — but it gives no team-sport outcome data; fitting a multi-day, deliberately
high-fatigue block inside a football game week specifically is untested here (see
[[framework--in-season-team-sport-mini-block-microcycle]] for the team-sport-adapted version).
**Eric's baseline:** the department explicitly treats glycolytic conditioning for football as
something to absorb incidentally through camp and practice rather than as a primary programmed
target (`method-baseline.md`, "Conditioning and energy systems," citing `class-4-2026.md`
pp.34, 39), a different posture than this microcycle's deliberate, concentrated glycolytic
emphasis, which is drawn from individual/dual/combat-sport programming. **Inference:** blood
lactate testing capability (needed to hit the stated mM zones precisely) is not named as a
standard part of the department's documented testing stack in this baseline corpus.

**Example** — **Inference:** a transmutation-mesocycle week built for a combat-sport or team-sport athlete
needing anaerobic capacity could place three key-workouts across the week (per Figure 3.5's
pattern, one each for anaerobic glycolytic power, anaerobic glycolytic capacity, and strength
endurance), buffered by an alactic-maintenance session, a mid-week restoration window, and
sessions blending anaerobic glycolytic power with strength endurance, accepting that athletes
will not be fully restored entering most of these sessions.

**Related** — [[framework--transmutation-mesocycle-duration-and-overtraining-monitoring]],
[[framework--in-season-team-sport-mini-block-microcycle]],
[[case-study--popov-aerobic-strength-microcycle]],
[[principle--training-modality-compatibility-in-a-workout]].

# Sedykh's Hammer-Throw Microcycle Puts Event-Specific Explosive Work Only in Morning, First-in-Session Slots

**What it is** — Issurin presents the eleven-workout microcycle of two-time Olympic champion
hammer thrower Yuri Sedykh (USSR), as reported by his coach (Bondarchuk, 1986) (PDF pp.
101-103, printed pp. 90-92, Table 3.4 and Figure 3.6). Four essential features: (a)
event-specific explosive-strength exercises (throwing different-weight hammers), the
top-priority target, appear **exclusively** in morning sessions and always in the **initial**
part of the workout, to use the athlete's most favorable physical state for the key-exercise;
(b) maximum-strength exercises (barbell snatch, half squats, good mornings), a supporting
role, are placed in five sessions: four separate evening sessions plus once in the second
part of a morning session; (c) additional explosive-strength work (standing jumps) appears
three times, "but not when the athlete was in his best condition" (the book's own wording;
the Tue PM standing-jump session follows a barbell max-strength session, not a throwing
session — it does not follow "the primary explosive work"); (d) restorative activity
(basketball, swimming, stretching) is built into the program, including on the day off.
Issurin also states that specialised strength exercises should duplicate the competition
technique: the coach must understand the throwing skill and build the strength exercise to
simulate it, so technique and strength improve together (Yessis, 2006, PDF p. 103, printed
p. 92). Issurin separately cites a
related mechanism study: Cardinale and Stone (2006) measured resting blood testosterone and
countermovement vertical jump in 70 elite athletes (48 men, 22 women; sprinters, handball,
volleyball, soccer) after a 10-hour fast and a rest day, finding a significant positive
relationship between testosterone and jump height (r = 0.61, p < 0.001) (PDF p. 104, printed
p. 93). Issurin's own stated implications from that study: athletes with relatively high
testosterone (either sex) have some inherited predisposition for explosive-strength
performance, and microcycle design for explosive-strength development should avoid excessive
fatigue, because fatigue suppresses testosterone and sharply reduces the training effect of
maximal-power exercises.

**Why it works** — Issurin's stated mechanism (PDF pp. 103-104, printed pp. 92-93) is that
explosive strength depends on the sensitivity
and reactivity of the neuromuscular system, and excessive fatigue "disrupts the subtle
regulation of neural input and muscle contraction"; testosterone is named as the hormone
determining strength training's anabolic effect and as an index of induced physical stress
(Viru and Viru, 2000). **Inference:** the placement rule (explosive work only when fresh,
morning, first in the session) follows directly from this same logic already generalized in
[[heuristic--exercise-sequencing-by-fatigue-state]]: CNS-dependent, high-precision qualities
need a well-rested athlete, and this case study is simply that general rule applied to one
specific, historically documented program.

**When to apply** — As a concrete illustration of sequencing explosive/technical power work
at the very start of a session, before any fatigue-inducing supporting work, for athletes
whose primary target ability is explosive strength in a highly coordinated skill.
**Inference:** in football, this maps most directly to skill-position or specialist
explosive-power development (e.g., jump-training or Olympic-lift-variant work meant to
transfer to explosive movement): placing that work first in a session, before conditioning
or high-volume accessory work, mirrors Sedykh's morning-first placement of hammer throws.

**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — This is a single elite thrower's program from a single
coach's secondhand report (Bondarchuk, 1986), with no comparison athlete or outcome data
beyond the general BPC narrative already logged in
[[case-study--bondarchuk-hammer-throw-block-mesocycles]]: it illustrates a design principle,
not a validated dose-response result. **Inference:** hammer throw is an acyclic, single-effort,
highly technical power event with no contact and no in-competition fatigue accumulation across
a "game," unlike football; the specific workout counts, throw counts, and session splits in
Table 3.4 should not be copied as a template. The testosterone-jump correlation (Cardinale and
Stone, 2006) is cross-sectional and observational (r = 0.61 explains well under half the
variance in jump height): it identifies an association at one time point in rested athletes,
not a training intervention; it does not establish that raising testosterone directly causes
higher jump performance, only that they covary. Population also spans track, handball,
volleyball and soccer athletes of both sexes, not football specifically. **Inference, from
the primary abstract (Cardinale & Stone, 2006, *JSCR* 20:103-107):** the r = 0.61 correlation
is computed on the pooled sample of men and women (n = 70) together. Women's resting
testosterone was reported at 9.5% of men's and their CMJ at 86.3% of men's, so a correlation
pooled across sexes largely reflects the sex difference in both variables rather than a
within-sex relationship. This undercuts Issurin's inference that athletes with high
testosterone "(both male and female)" individually carry "some inherited predisposition" for
explosive-strength performance; the entry's caveat above (cross-sectional, observational)
does not by itself capture this confound.

**Example** — **Inference:** a football skill player's Tuesday lift built around explosive-power development
(e.g., trap-bar jumps, medicine-ball throws) should be sequenced first in the session, on a day
following adequate rest, with any high-volume or fatiguing accessory work placed afterward,
not the reverse.

**Related** — [[heuristic--exercise-sequencing-by-fatigue-state]],
[[case-study--bondarchuk-hammer-throw-block-mesocycles]],
[[framework--key-workout-and-key-exercise-concept]].

# Accumulation Mesocycle: Up to Six Weeks for Deep Change, Three Weeks or Less to Refresh, 10-14 Days Late-Season

**What it is** — This is the full prescriptive detail behind the accumulation block first
introduced conceptually in [[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]]
(Ch. 1). Issurin gives duration as a function of two competing factors (PDF pp. 113-115,
printed pp. 102-104): the time needed for a real cumulative training effect in the targeted
basic abilities, aerobic endurance and maximal strength, both requiring "profound morphological
and even organic changes," versus the time limit the competition calendar allows. He cites a
supporting case study: eight highly qualified female kayakers, monitored over a **20-week**
program of high-resistance training (**4-5 hr/week**) aimed at maximal strength and aerobic
endurance, tracked via maximal isometric force in kayak-specific positions (Figure 3.9, PDF p.
114, printed p. 103, based on Sharobajko, 1984). Strength gain and weekly improvement rate fell
sharply over time: the first 3 weeks produced a 5.9% average gain (the book prints this as a 1.93%/week
improvement rate; arithmetically 5.9% over 3 weeks is 1.97%/week — recorded here as a source
quirk, not corrected); the next 3 weeks added only 1.6% more (0.53%/week); the remaining 14
weeks added only 0.25% and then 0.13% per week. Issurin's stated conclusion: the fitness
program was "very effective at the beginning, reasonably effective through the first six
weeks, and had only a minor effect for the next 14 weeks," directly supporting BPC's case for
shorter, higher-turnover blocks over long, continuous ones. The general adaptive-decline
concept itself is cited to Bouchard (1986); the further claim that aerobic-endurance programs
show "similar trends" is given uncited in the text (PDF p. 115, printed p. 104). Based on this,
Issurin sets the following duration bands (PDF p. 115, printed p. 104): **up to six weeks**
when training is intended to elicit "more profound physiological changes" (typically early
season, when athletes are less calendar-constrained); **three weeks or less** when training is
intended "to stimulate basic abilities and refresh general responses"; **10-14 days** at
season's end, when important competitions come at short intervals. Content is structured by
sequencing microcycle types (Table 3.7, PDF p. 116, printed p. 105; re-verified against the
page image, 2026-09-27): the **initial** part uses a restoration microcycle (if starting a new

# Competition Cut Popov's Aerobic-Mesocycle Gains Roughly in Half (V-AT) Within About Ten Days

**What it is** — Issurin addresses whether competitions inside a training stage (not the
final target competition) help or hurt (PDF pp. 128-129, printed pp. 117-118). His position:
mid- and low-level competitions inside accumulation or transmutation mesocycles add useful
emotional diversity and elicit training responses that enrich adaptation, but highly intense
competitive efforts also trigger a stress-hormone response. The supporting case: Alexander
Popov's (Russia, multi-Olympic/World swimming champion) preparation was tracked with an
incremental stepwise swimming test measuring anaerobic threshold speed, V-AT (blood lactate =
4 mM) and V-La8, the speed producing 8 mM lactate (the stated lower limit of highly intense
glycolytic work). Measurements were taken at the start of a highly concentrated aerobic
mesocycle, again 10 days later, and again a few days after Popov competed several times
(Figure 3.11, PDF p. 129, printed p. 118; re-verified against the page image, 2026-09-27,
adapted from Pyne & Touretski, 1993). Both velocity markers rose over the mesocycle's first
~10 days (V-AT 1.57 to 1.63 m/s; V-La8 1.64 to 1.72 m/s), then fell after the competition
(V-AT to 1.60 m/s at day ~21; V-La8 to 1.70 m/s), a decline the book itself calls "a
substantial decrease" — its own wording, not "erased" or "fatigued." About half of the V-AT
gain and about a quarter of the V-La8 gain were lost; both markers remain above their starting
values. Issurin attributes this decline to shortened training residuals "induced by the
previous program" (PDF p. 128, printed p. 117), i.e. to the competition's effect on the
residual clock, not to any stated change in the training content itself.

**Why it works — the author's own attributed mechanism, not independently re-derived here** —
The book gives two separate chains, not one merged chain (PDF p. 128, printed p. 117): (a)
stress hormones (catecholamines, cortisol) reinforce the catabolic process (Viru & Viru, 2001),
so "muscle mass and maximum strength can decrease"; and (b), cited to a different source,
"the highly intense anaerobic glycolitic efforts typical in competition suppress the activity
of aerobic enzymes and the oxidative process in the mitochondria" (Volkov, 1986). The book's
conclusion 3 (PDF p. 129, printed p. 118) ties the shortened residual to stress hormones in
general; Volkov is specifically the citation behind the glycolytic-suppression chain (b), not
the hormonal chain (a). **Inference:** chain (b) is the same physiological substrate underlying
aerobic endurance's normal ~30-day residual
(see [[claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]]), so a hard competition can
be read as an accelerant on that decay clock rather than a separate, independent event; the
book does not state this link explicitly. Issurin also notes the field's practical response:
"prominent coaches" have "added special aerobic workloads to restore and revitalize the
athletes after competition" (PDF p. 128, printed p. 117), a plain author statement, not this
entry's own inference.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** as a citable, named-athlete illustration for why a program including
in-season or in-training-stage competitive tests should expect some real cost to basic-ability
residuals, not treat competing as a free additional training stimulus. Directly supports the
caution already logged for the transmutation mesocycle
(see [[framework--transmutation-mesocycle-duration-and-overtraining-monitoring]]) about why
"including competition" is listed as an *option*, with tradeoffs, rather than an unqualified
recommendation. **Inference:** for football, this is a reason to expect that a physically
brutal, high-intensity early-season or mid-season game can measurably eat into whatever aerobic
or strength base was built in the preceding weeks, not just add acute fatigue that resolves in
a few days, which argues for the mini-block "topping up" logic in
[[framework--prolonging-residual-effects-with-mini-blocks]] being applied proactively after
unusually hard, high-intensity games, not only on a fixed calendar schedule.

**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — This is a single elite swimmer's data, reported secondhand
(Pyne & Touretski, 1993, published via Issurin & Lustig, 2004), with no comparison athlete who
trained the same mesocycle without competing, and no statistical test of the pre/post-competition
change reported in this text: the chart (Figure 3.11) shows one athlete's trajectory, not a
group result. **Inference:** swimming's anaerobic-threshold/lactate-based test protocol has no
direct football analog; football has no simple single-modality repeated field test that isolates
"aerobic threshold" the way a stepwise swim test does, so this exact monitoring approach cannot
be copied, only the underlying caution (hard competition costs some residual) can be carried
over. This case does not address whether the effect is dose-dependent on competition intensity,
duration, or the athlete's fitness level entering the competition.

**Example** — **Inference:** a strength staff noting that a physically demanding, high-effort game (e.g., a
triple-overtime contest, or a game following an unusually taxing travel/short-week schedule)
likely cost the team some of the conditioning base built the prior weeks has a named precedent
(Popov's threshold-speed decline) for treating that as a real, not just anecdotal, training-load
event worth a deliberate light aerobic "top-up" in the following week, rather than assuming a
normal recovery day fully addresses it.

**Related** — [[claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]],
[[framework--transmutation-mesocycle-duration-and-overtraining-monitoring]],
[[framework--prolonging-residual-effects-with-mini-blocks]],
[[case-study--popov-aerobic-strength-microcycle]].

# A Two-Mini-Block Weekly Structure for In-Season Team Sports, Naming American Football Directly

**What it is** — Issurin addresses the specific constraint that team and dual sports (he
names **soccer, American football, rugby, volleyball** explicitly) run a 20-35 week season
where "the possibility of inserting highly concentrated training blocks is very limited"
(PDF pp. 108-109, printed pp. 97-98). He cites Fleck and Kraemer (1997): players typically
maintain strength near pre-season levels for 14-16 weeks, after which strength variables
decrease dramatically. Because the usual one-week gap between games is too short to work
effectively on every training target (metabolic conditioning, maximal/explosive strength,
injury prevention, techno-tactical skill, game-specific endurance, active restoration) at once,
Issurin proposes adapting three BPC approaches at the *week* level: high concentration of
specialized workloads within **mini-blocks**, separating mini-blocks by training modality, and
determining **key-workouts** within each mini-block. The worked example (Figure 3.8, PDF p.
109, printed p. 98, "based on Baker, 2001," a real cited source, not an uncited synthesis)
splits a standard Monday-Sunday week into two mini-blocks. **Mini-block 1 (Monday-Wednesday)**
targets sport-specific maximal and explosive strength as the dominant training aim: it opens
Monday with an active-recovery session (medium/low load, aerobic and general conditioning),
then delivers the strength emphasis across **two key-workouts** (Tuesday and Wednesday
mornings, maximal strength plus explosive strength as the secondary modality), combined with a
medium-load team practice (Tuesday afternoon) and a conditioning-restorative workout
(Wednesday afternoon). This sequencing leaves **28-30 hours of recovery** after the Wednesday
strength key-workout before mini-block 2's team-practice key-workout begins, to let the
anabolic/restorative process run before the next demand.
**Mini-block 2 (Thursday-Saturday)** targets sport-specific team practice and immediate game
preparation: it includes two obligatory team practices, one before the day off (Thursday
afternoon, itself the microcycle's **third key-workout**, "substantial or big" load, intended
to deliver a pronounced game-specific stimulus) and a second, load-restricted session
immediately before the game itself (Saturday, mostly techno-tactical drills tied to the
specific forthcoming opponent) — Figure 3.8 shows a total of three key-workouts across the
week, not two. Issurin notes some highly motivated teams skip the day off and add an optional
Friday-morning conditioning or techno-tactical session instead, trading recovery time for
extra preparation; he states the tradeoff explicitly without endorsing either choice. The
chart gives priority to maximal-strength development over explosive-type work within the week,
which Issurin explains as protecting "somatic, functional and anabolic status," while noting a
cited counter-example (Newton et al., 2006) of sequencing classic high-resistance training with
ballistic explosive-type microcycles to enhance jump performance instead.

**Why it works** — Issurin's own stated reason (PDF p. 111, printed p. 100): weekly
competition stress "restrict[s] the benefits of utilizing BP mesocycle sequencing. However,
the benefits of accentuating dominant training targets, in a mini-block structure, and
designing key-workouts can be attained." **Inference:** this is the chapter's direct answer to
the constraint stated in [[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]] (BPC needs
concentrated, sequenced blocks) meeting the constraint that team sports cannot suspend
competition long enough to run full-length accumulation/transmutation/realization mesocycles
(see [[framework--accumulation-mesocycle-duration-and-monitoring]] and
[[framework--transmutation-mesocycle-duration-and-overtraining-monitoring]] for what those
normally require in duration); splitting the week itself into two purpose-specific mini-blocks,
each with its own key-workouts, is a way of keeping some of BPC's concentration benefit even
though the underlying block can only be one week long, not several, but the author frames it
as attaining benefits under a restriction, not as a full substitute for mesocycle sequencing.

**When to apply — this is the entry most directly answering the in-season half of the
strength-and-conditioning miss-log's "peaking phase structure for collegiate football" gap
(logged 2026-09-03)** — Issurin explicitly names American football as a sport this structure
is meant for. **Eric's baseline's** in-season rule, "maintain intensity, reduce volume"
(`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power," citing `01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md`
pp.20-21), is compatible with and gets a concrete weekly shape from this framework: the
early-week mini-block is where intensity (maximal/explosive strength) gets its two key-workouts,
while the late-week mini-block is deliberately techno-tactical and load-restricted heading into
the game, which *is* the volume reduction the baseline rule calls for. **Inference:** the
28-30 hour recovery window between the strength mini-block and the practice-heavy mini-block
gives a specific, citable number for how much gap a college program might target between its
heaviest in-season lift and the next high-intensity team session; Issurin does not himself
generalize this figure beyond the Figure 3.8 worked example.

**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — The specific day-by-day chart (Figure 3.8) is built from
one cited source, Baker (2001), a study of professional and college-aged rugby league players'
in-season concurrent training: a real, checkable citation, but a single study in rugby league,
a sport with a different weekly game/practice rhythm than college football, which layers
additional constraints (NCAA-mandated practice-time limits, travel, and a Saturday-only game
schedule rather than rugby league's varying weekly structure). **Population caveat:** none of
this section's evidence comes from American football itself; Issurin lists
football alongside soccer, rugby, and volleyball as sports the *problem* applies to, but the
worked example and its supporting citation are rugby-specific. **Inference:** the specific
"two key-workouts, 28-30 hours recovery" prescription should be treated as a structural
template to adapt to football's own practice-count and padded/unpadded-practice rules, not a
ready-made in-season lift schedule. Issurin gives no guidance here for bye weeks, short
(Thursday-game) weeks, or the postseason gap before a bowl game; those fall outside this
weekly-cycle framework and are closer to the pre-competitive/realization material in
[[framework--pre-competitive-microcycle-tuning]] and
[[framework--prolonging-residual-effects-with-mini-blocks]].

**Example** — **Inference, following Figure 3.8's actual pattern (PDF p. 109, printed p. 98)
for a Sunday game:** Monday AM active recovery/conditioning; Tuesday AM maximal-strength
key-workout (plus explosive strength), Tuesday PM medium-load team practice; Wednesday AM
second maximal-strength key-workout (plus explosive strength, bigger load), Wednesday PM
active-recovery/conditioning; Thursday PM key team practice (substantial-to-big load); Friday
off; Saturday AM team practice/technical work (medium load); game Sunday. For a Saturday-game
week, this pattern would need to shift roughly one day earlier across the board (e.g., the two
strength key-workouts moving to Sunday-Monday and the key team practice to Wednesday), since
Issurin's own worked example assumes a Sunday game and does not itself address the shift.

**Related** — [[framework--microcycle-types-and-load-wave-design]],
[[framework--pre-competitive-microcycle-tuning]],
[[heuristic--two-a-day-workout-sequencing-by-dominant-ability]],
[[claim--morning-resistance-training-no-decrement-after-6hr-rest]],
[[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]].

   correspondence coupling point. Labelled the Example `Inference:`.

   mechanism as plain quoted text (incompatible-systems conflict, 2-3 day hormonal shift, Viru
   1995) and the Zatsiorsky (1985) strength-trade-off sentence. Labelled the Ch1
   interference-case link `Inference:` and fixed its direction (that case is aerobic suppressing

   invented "rather than only in the weight room" clause. Scoped the 24-hour rule to developing
   max-strength work specifically, against Figure 3.4's actual same-day/next-day placements.

   shift Issurin's own example does not address. Fixed "mesocycles" to "microcycles" (Newton
   2006 citation). Added the Thursday team practice as the week's third key-workout. Replaced
   the invented "why it works" synthesis with Issurin's own stated reason (PDF p. 111, printed
   p. 100) and labelled the rest `Inference:`. Labelled the last When to apply sentence
   `Inference:`.
